description: Mangrove forests provide critical coastal flood protection, yet their ongoing loss in combination with sea level rise creates a compounding exposure dynamic that remains poorly quantified at sub-national scale across Southeast Asia. This study presents the first systematic, multi-decadal analysis of mangrove loss and coastal flood exposure change for the 10 km coastal buffer of East Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak), covering 1996 to 2020 and projecting forward to 2050 under a structured scenario matrix. Drawing on five openly available global datasets — the Global Mangrove Watch v3.0, Copernicus GLO-30 digital elevation model, WorldPop 2020 population grid, GADM v4.1 administrative boundaries, and IPCC AR6 sea level projections — and a reproducible Python-based workflow, the study quantifies mangrove extent change, hydrologically-connected inundation zones at five elevation thresholds, flood exposure attributable to historical loss, and population exposure under six combined mangrove loss and sea level rise scenarios. Net mangrove loss of 46.34 km² (−1.14%) was recorded over the study period, masking a gross loss of 114.06 km². Four spatial hotspots were identified: the Rajang Delta, SW Sarawak coast, Menumbok Forest Reserve and Kinabatangan coast. Historical mangrove loss exposed an additional 43.79 to 52.14 km² of coastline to inundation, affecting approximately 10,200 to 12,730 people. Scenario projections to 2050 demonstrate that mangrove management trajectory exerts a substantially greater influence on future flood exposure than the choice of emissions scenario, with the spread across mangrove loss scenarios (~31 km², ~13,400 people) exceeding the SSP2-4.5 to SSP5-8.5 spread by more than an order of magnitude. These findings underscore the value of mangrove conservation as a near-term, nature-based coastal adaptation measure in the Indo-Pacific region. Keywords: Mangrove loss; coastal flood exposure; sea level rise; East Malaysia; nature-based adaptation; inundation modelling; blue carbon Article highlights: Net mangrove loss of 46.34 km² recorded in East Malaysia's coastal buffer, 1996–2020 Four loss hotspots identified including the Rajang Delta and Menumbok Forest Reserve Historical loss exposed 43.79–52.14 km² of additional coastline to inundation risk Mangrove management trajectory dominates over SLR scenario choice at 2050 horizon Reproducible open-source workflow transferable to other Indo-Pacific mangrove coastlines

GLC_FCS60 is the first global 60-m land cover product with a fine classification system developed using comprehensive change detection. It employs a refined classification system inherited from the GLC_FCS30D product, which contains 35 land-cover classes and covers the years 1975 and 1980. Specifically, it is developed by combining an improved comprehensive change detection method, local adaptive classification models, and a series of post-classification processing methods, primarily using Landsat MSS time-series imagery. Validation results show that the 1975 product achieves overall accuracies of 80.13% for the 10 basic classes and 71.60% for the 17 level-1 classes, whereas the 1980 product achieves corresponding accuracies of 80.08% and 70.71%, respectively. The GLC_FCS60 dataset has been stored by a total of 961 independent 5°×5° geographical tiles, and the tile names as “GLC_FCS60_19751980_E***N##”, in which the “***” and “##” illustrate the longitude and latitude coordinates of the upper left corner of the tile data.

In the past 15 years, solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) has been retrieved from spaceborne remote sensing instruments destined for atmospheric studies. This retrieved variable has shown an apparently strong linear relationship with gross primary productivity (GPP) at the global scale, suggesting a strong potential to establish satellite-based estimations of ecosystem productivity. However, this relationship is not consistent across ecosystems and can break down under stress conditions, raising limitation about its application. The relationship is known to vary with respect to radiation intensity, vegetation structure and physiological conditions. Thus, it has been proposed to reason in terms of quantum efficiency of SIF (SIF yield, φF), rather than SIF itself, in order to isolate the physiological signal that should give the additional information regarding GPP that is not already get from vegetation indices combined with radiation. In this experimental product developed within NextGenCarbon, we are combining difference sources of satellite remote sensing to try to establish a weekly product of φF at European scale. We are providing a first prototype of what this product will look like. It will then be improved during the course of the project towards a final refined product.

description: The integrated dataset represents the synthesis of all deliverables produced within the framework of the Interreg Italy-Croatia project CRESCO Adria-Climate Resilient Coastal Planning in the Adriatic (https://www.italy-croatia.eu/web/crescoadria) for the New Pescara pilot case (Pescara, Montesilvano and Spoltore). It does not constitute a standalone product, but rather a component of a single, integrated analytical process. The thematic GIS datasets developed for the pilot area were produced within a common spatial framework and according to harmonised classification schemes. Taken together, they provide the hazard, exposure and territorial transformation components underpinning the integrated territorial diagnosis. Individual layers are normalised and combined into a composite territorial risk index, subsequently analysed using Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) to identify statistically significant clusters of risk, and interpreted to assign a Climate Adaptation Territorial Profile to each analysis cell. These profiles are then inherited by the Territorial Planning Units generated through the aggregation of contiguous cells sharing the same classification. The morpho-climatic characterisation is based on the Local Climate Zones (LCZ) classification, which partitions the urban and peri-urban environment into homogeneous classes according to urban morphology, building density, building height and land-cover characteristics. Interpreted together with indicators of soil sealing and building density, the LCZ framework captures the thermal and hydrological behaviour of different urban contexts and contributes to the diagnostic conditions underpinning the classification. Spatial entropy measures are used to evaluate the degree of local homogeneity and identify transitional areas characterised by greater spatial complexity. Accordingly, each dataset retains its own thematic and documentary value, while its full significance emerges only when considered as part of the complete integrated series. Collectively, these datasets support the transition from climate risk assessment to the operational planning of climate adaptation measures for the New Pescara pilot area.
keywords: flood exposure; urban resilience; climate-resilient flood management; GIS; CRESCO Adria

description: version update 06 July 2026: corrected erroneous area data in OceanSODA fCO2-product. -- Surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs) and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products). There are three types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series, (2) one file per GOBM and simulation with gridded fields, and (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2025 (https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025), are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2025 spreadsheet. The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2024 paper (https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025), the river flux adjustment needs to be added to the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2025 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Two of the 9 fCO2-producst (i.e. JMA-MLR and UExP-FNN-U) include a temperature adjustment to correct the the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) What is in the files? description: The Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUH2) dataset is updated every year for use in the annual Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations and publications. The LUH2-GCB2026 dataset represents the land-use data used by DGVMs and book-keeping models in the GCB 2026. It is extended to the current year using new input data from FAO and other sources, and extends historical trends for years without underlying input data. In particular, it incorporates new HYDE land-use data as a key input, continues to provide improved representation of deforestation in Brazil and Indonesia by using the latest versions of MapBiomas remote sensing data, and it improves cropland areas in China using data from Yu et al. 2022. The Global Mangrove Watch (GMW; https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) v4.1 timeseries layers were generated using the full Landsat and Sentinel-2 timeseries and available JAXA L-band data (JERS-1, ALOS PALSAR, ALOS-2 PALSAR-2). The methodology is built on knowledge gained from developing the previous GMW layers (GMW v2.0, GMW v3.0, and GMW v4.0). Building on the GMW v4.0 10m baseline for defining the reference data, the GMW v4.1 timeseries used multiple baseline years (1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025), with classifications created using an XGBoost classifier and composites of Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery. Areas of missing data due to the availability of Landsat imagery were copied through from the nearest year. These baselines were visually checked, and for 1985, 1990, and 1995, areas of poor quality were copied using the base quality and the earliest available layer. Subsequently, these baselines were filtered into a timeseries using a Markov chain with probabilities defined for the transitions. To create the annual timeseries, every Landsat and Sentinel-2 scene with less than 70% cloud cover was classified using 130 random forest classifiers in Google Earth Engine and summarised on an annual basis with the number of valid pixel observations and the number of times the pixel was classified as mangroves. These classifications were combined with thresholded JAXA L-band SAR data and the baseline classifications using a likelihood ratio methodology to define a probability of a pixel being mangroves for each year in the timeseries. The subsequent timeseries was then filtered using Bayesian updating and Markov chains, with the output probabilities thresholded to define the final mangrove extent maps. Throughout, extensive visual quality assurance (QA) checks were integrated, and the layers were updated based on the feedback. The accuracy assessment for the mangrove extent estimated a global F1-Score of 0.9276 (0.9220 - 0.9330), with an omission of 6.357% (5.648 - 7.133) and a commission of 8.093% (7.093 - 9.128). This accuracy assessment was based on 32,569 reference points distributed across 120 geographic sites covering the full range of years within the analysis. Therefore, these accuracy statistics represent the average for the product and will vary locally in both time and geography. Where errors are identified and can be fed back to the developers, those errors can be improved in future versions of the GMW timeseries. It is important to be aware that the timeseries is dependent on the availability of satellite imagery, and before 1999/2000, the availability of imagery can be significantly reduced. This problem increases the further back in time you go. To provide full coverage on an annual basis throughout the timeseries, this has required some infilling of data from other years, particularly in the 1990s and 1980s. These data and statistics are available through the Global Mangrove Watch portal (https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org), along with further mangrove related data layers and products, such as blue carbon and restoration potential. We will continue to update these layers with additional years and improvements. If and when errors or data issues are encountered, please provide feedback to help us improve them. We maintain an issue tracker on GitHub: https://github.com/globalmangrovewatch/gmw_mangrove_extent

description: These are the country boundaries which are used by the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) for calculating mangrove statistics. The country boundaries were primarily extracted from Open Street Map but then edited to meet the needs of the GMW. The GMW reports both countries and territories. For example, European overseas territories are reported individually rather than as the overseas territory. Mangroves are tricky as they straddle the coastal boundary and therefore a coastal buffer is included to ensure that all mangrove regions are captured. We have identified disputed regions (e.g., the Hala'ib Triangle) as separate regions, and therefore, the end user can allocate these areas to the country or territory as a post-processing step. description: This article analyzes the impact of improving energy efficiency in thermal power plants of Uzbekistan on electricity generation volume and carbon dioxide () emissions. The study investigates the technical and economic performance indicators of thermal power plants, which constitute the main generation capacity within the country’s power system. The relationship between thermal efficiency, fuel consumption, and electricity generation was evaluated using mathematical methods. The findings demonstrate that increasing energy efficiency reduces natural gas consumption and, consequently, decreases emissions. Furthermore, the effects of modern combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) units, high-efficiency turbines, and digital control technologies on energy efficiency were assessed. The results indicate that modernizing thermal power plants in Uzbekistan plays a crucial role in strengthening energy security, ensuring the rational use of fuel resources, and reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas emissions.

description: The Global Dam Image Dataset (GDID) is a publicly available dataset developed for training and evaluating deep learning models for multispectral image generation and dam construction analysis. Since no public dataset previously provided paired multispectral images acquired before dam construction and after the first reservoir impoundment together with corresponding guidance masks, GDID was created to address this gap. The dataset was generated using information from the Global Dam Watch (GDW) database, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 imagery (Landsat 4–9), Google Earth Engine (GEE), OpenStreetMap, the GLC_FCS30D and Dynamic World land-cover datasets, and a newly developed Detection of Initial Reservoir Impoundment (DIRI) algorithm. DIRI estimates the first reservoir impoundment year by analyzing long-term surface water dynamics within the reservoir extent. Each sample contains: • A six-band multispectral Landsat image acquired before dam construction. • A corresponding six-band multispectral image acquired after the first reservoir impoundment. • A guidance mask indicating the dam crest, reservoir area, and background. All images have a spatial size of 512 × 512 pixels (covering 15.36 × 15.36 km²) and include the Red, Green, Blue, NIR, SWIR1, and SWIR2 bands normalized to the range [0, 1]. The guidance masks were generated using NDWI-based water extraction and land-cover information, followed by manual refinement to ensure accurate reservoir and dam crest boundaries. After quality control and manual verification, the final dataset contains 2,188 training samples and 546 testing samples. GDID is intended for research on remote sensing image generation, conditional generative models, dam monitoring, reservoir analysis, and related Earth observation applications.
keywords: Deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Machine Learning; Computer Vision; Dam; Satellite Imagery

description: Description The spatial delineation of managed and unmanaged land is essential for ensuring consistency between spatial datasets (e.g. remote sensing products and atmospheric greenhouse gas inversions) and national GHG inventory reporting under the UNFCCC. According to the recent National Inventory Document (NID, 2025), managed land in Russian Federation accounts for 940 million ha, or 56% of the total land area. This dataset provides a spatially explicit delineation of managed and unmanaged land across Russia for the year 2020. It is specifically designed to support comparison between spatial datasets and national inventory reporting. The classification is based on a combination of global land cover products and auxiliary datasets. The ESA WorldCover 2021 dataset (Zanaga et al., 2022) was used as the base land cover map. Methodology Unmanaged land was identified based on the following criteria: Forests without management plans (155.5 million ha, NID, 2025) Delineated based on regional forest management plan data (HCVF, 2025). Natural grasslands (18.2 million ha) Derived from ESA WorldCover grassland class (class 20), excluding managed grasslands using Global Pasture Watch (Parente et al., 2025). Undisturbed wetlands (including inner waters: 226.5 million ha) Identified from ESA WorldCover wetland-related classes (class 90), as well as grasslands and shrublands (classes 20 and 30) consistent with national wetland map (Schepaschenko, Shvidenko, 2026). Managed and modified areas were excluded using WPC (2026). Natural water bodies Derived from ESA WorldCover (class 80), excluding reservoirs identified using the Global Dam Watch database (GDW, 2024). Other unmanaged land (359.5 million ha), Including: Bare land, snow, and ice (ESA WorldCover classes 60, 70) Tundra ecosystems (ESA WorldCover classes 20, 30, 100), excluding managed grasslands (Parente et al., 2025) Abandoned afforested land, defined as forest cover (class 10) on previously abandoned cropland (Lesiv et al., 2018) All remaining areas were classified as managed land. Additional adjustments were applied: Mining areas (Maus et al., 2020) were classified as managed land Bare land adjacent to built-up areas was also assigned to managed land Output Data The final product is land management classification and a binary raster mask of managed and unmanaged land in the Russian Federation for the year 2020. The dataset is provided at a spatial resolution of approximately 100 m (0.000833 degrees) in the WGS 84 geographic coordinate system. References GDW (2024). description: The Global Dam Image Dataset Version 1.0 (GDID V1.0) is a publicly available global dataset developed to support research on environmental monitoring, change detection, assessment of environmental changes associated with dam construction, and decision-making related to dam development. The dataset provides temporally paired multispectral observations acquired before and after dam construction, together with spatial guidance information describing dam crests and reservoir areas and a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for each sample. GDID V1.0 was developed by integrating information from multiple data sources, including the Global Dam Watch database, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Tier-1 imagery from Landsat 4–9, Google Earth Engine, OpenStreetMap, the GLC_FCS30D and Dynamic World land-cover datasets, and the Detection of Initial Reservoir Impoundment (DIRI) algorithm developed in this study. DIRI was used to estimate the year of first reservoir impoundment based on long-term surface-water dynamics within the spatial extent of each reservoir. Each GDID V1.0 sample consists of four components: (1) a six-band pre-construction multispectral Landsat image; (2) a corresponding six-band post-construction multispectral Landsat image acquired after the first reservoir impoundment; (3) a guidance mask delineating the dam crest, reservoir area, and background; and (4) a DEM corresponding to the same spatial extent as the multispectral images. The multispectral images have a spatial dimension of 512 × 512 pixels, corresponding to a ground coverage of 15.36 × 15.36 km². Each image contains six spectral bands: Red, Green, Blue, Near-Infrared (NIR), Shortwave Infrared 1 (SWIR1), and Shortwave Infrared 2 (SWIR2). The guidance masks were generated using NDWI-based surface-water extraction and land-cover information and were subsequently reviewed and manually refined to improve the spatial correspondence of reservoir boundaries and dam crests with the Landsat imagery. The DEM data were spatially aligned with the corresponding multispectral images. Following image quality assessment, visual inspection, and data refinement, GDID V1.0 contains 5,685 samples. The dataset is publicly available and provides a comprehensive data resource for studies involving dam-related environmental change analysis, remote sensing, reservoir monitoring, and Earth observation applications.
keywords: deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Machine Learning; Computer Vision; Dam; Satellite Imagery

description: This dataset supports the study "Flood Gradient-Driven Coupling Differentiation of Soil-Vegetation-Water Systems in Temperate Fluvial Floodplains: A Case Study of the Liaohe River (Shenyang Section)". The scripts generate: (1) flood-season cumulative inundation frequency from Sentinel-1 GRD imagery (VH polarization, IW mode, VH < -20 dB threshold); (2) growing-season maximum NDVI and fractional vegetation cover (FVC) from Sentinel-2 L2A imagery (QA60 cloud masking, endmembers 0.70/0.05); (3) land use from ESA WorldCover v200; and (4) soil texture (sand, silt, clay) from OpenLandMap v02. The file Sample_Points_v3_FullExport.csv contains 1995 sample points with 12 fields, including inundation frequency (%), FVC, soil texture components, land use, topographic wetness index (TWI), coupling coordination degree (D), and flood zone class. Raw remote sensing products are publicly available through Google Earth Engine; derived rasters were processed in ArcGIS Pro. Analyses reported in the paper used 1799 complete cases after excluding missing values and water pixels.

description: This is a dataset designed to provide geospatial layers of Urban Water Producing Systems in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Files RSH_WPS.gpkg -- geospatial database with layers preview_wps.png -- preview of layers Main layers rsh_wps_intake_surface -- 216 points of urban water intake filtered for surface waters. rsh_wps_intake_surface_catchments -- 216 polygon catchments related to each urban water intake point. Auxiliary layers rsh_wps_intake_all -- points of urban water intake of all forms (surface and groundwater). Source: Atlas Agua (ANA, 2021) rsh_wps_hydrosheds_drainage_v10 -- HydroSHEDS drainage network rsh_wps_hydrosheds_catchments_lev12 -- HydroSHEDS catchment grid level 12 rsh_wps_hydrosheds_catchments_lev08 -- HydroSHEDS catchment grid level 8 Methods The catchment polygons are the main novel output for these dataset. The catchments were delineated via a fast-algorithm that uses topological network analysis and raster DEM processing for fine-tuning. Geometries and areas are estimated and subject to revision. Script for the catchment definition: https://github.com/iporepos/get-catchments-fast Version logic v{Method Change}.{Major Change}.{Minor Change} Example: v1.2.4 Version history: v1.0.0 -- first release

Product Information Product name UExP-FNN-U SOCOM-style name UExP-FNN-U Product version v2026-1 Changelog at end of repository Coverage January 1980 – December 2025 Global ocean (including under ice regions) at ~0.2 m depth Resolution Monthly 1° x 1° Contact Daniel J. Ford d.ford@exeter.ac.uk Jamie D. Shutler j.d.shutler@exeter.ac.uk Traceable code and inputs Information on the input datasets and code can be found after the changelog How to reference these data? If these data are used please reference Ford et al. (2024a) and this repository with the version (the version is key to tracability). Note: If you use these data for a new analysis or publication, please contact Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk). This will allow the opportunity to contribute with detailed information on the dataset and depending on the level of involvement be considered for co-authorship. Product Description The UExP-FNN-U approach is described in detail within Ford et al. (2024a) and therefore we provide a summary of the algorithm for interpolating the fugacity of CO2 in seawater (fCO2 (sw)). The UExP-FNN-U is a two step neural network interpolation technique, the self-organising map feed forward neural network (SOM-FNN) (Landschützer et al., 2014, 2016). The first step is a self-organising map (SOM) which was used to divide the global oceans into regions, or provinces, of similar oceanic conditions. The inputs to this step were monthly climatology of sea surface temperature (SST) from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (ESA-CCI) SST, merged sea surface salinity (SSS) from the CCI and the CMEMS reanalysis (GLORYS12V1; merged using a hierarchy approach described in Gregor et al., 2024), CMEMS GLORYS12V1 mixed layer dapth (MLD), and spatailly and temporally complete OC-CCI chlorophyll-a (chl-a) (Ford et al. 2026a; Sathyendranath et al. 2019) and the Takahashi et al. (2009) fCO2 (sw) climatology updated in Fay et al. (2024). The SOM produces 16 provinces, and two manual provinces are implemented to cover the Arctic Ocean and Mediterranean + Red Sea using Longhurst biogeochemical provinces (Longhurst, 1998). The second step uses a feed forward neural network (FNN) ensemble (10 members) for each province to estimate the relationships between the target variable (i.e in situ fCO2 (sw) from the recalculated SOCAT dataset; Bakker et al., 2016; Ford et al., 2025; Ford et al. 2026c) and oceanic properties that likely control their variability. For the UExP-FNN-U v2026-pre1 these were SST, SSS, MLD, chl-a and xCO2 (atm) and anomalies of each. In v2026-pre1, we implemented a probability based SOM approach, which provides a probability that each monthly 1 degree pixel is assigned to each of the 18 provinces. To achieve the probabilities, the SOM training occurs as in Ford et al. (2024a) and then the inputs are perturbed within the limits of their uncertainties and the resulting SOM provinces retrieved for 400 ensembles. The probability that each monhtly 1 degree regions fall within a province are calculated. If a province probability is found to be less than 5%, this is set to 0 % to reduce computation. Locations where the sum of the probability is greater than 1 or less than 1 are scaled linearly to equal 1. In the FNN training stage the provinces are defined for the initial SOM (i.e the hard provinces that the SOM predicts with the data unperturbed). In the mapping stage the fCO2 (sw) and the uncertainties are predicted for each location and province, and a weighted sum of the resulting fCO2 (sw) and uncertainties is taken. This approach was shown to reduce large biases at the edge of provinces and reduced the appearance of provinces in the geographical outputs within a model testbed approach within the Surface Ocean CO2 mapping intercomparison (SOCOMv2 Experiment 2; Roobaret et al. 2026). Additionally, the global ocean CO2 sink for v2026-pre1 using the standard SOM approach as in Ford et al. (2024a) compared to this updated probability approach showed only minor differences (~2%). We have used this same probability based apporach in v2026-1. Expansion to Total Alkalinity using a consistent SOM-FNN The UExP-FNN-U approach was expanded to estimate Total Alkalinity (TA) on the same monthly 1 degree grid. The first step, the SOM, was trained on a monthly climatology of CCI-SST, CCI+CMEMS SSS and an annual TA climatology (DIVA interpolated in situ TA). Gregor and Gruber (2021) use the gridded GLODAPv2.2016 surface TA field for this step, but these have not been updated in recent years. Therefore, we use a merged in situ TA dataset produced from observations in GLODAPv3 (Lange et al. submitted) , SNAP-O-CO2v2 and Sharkweb datasets to produce a surface TA annual climatology using DIVA interpolation (Schlitzer and Reiner 2025). Data are currently too sparse to produce a monthly climatology of TA (highlighted in Gregor and Gruber; 2021). The SOM produces 16 provinces for the second FNN step, and there were no manual province modifications for TA. For the FNN step, as described in Gregor and Gruber (2021) the available TA observations are much lower than that for fCO2 (sw). Gridding the TA observations onto a monthly 1 degree grid before input into the UExP-FNN-U would greatly reduce the available constraints. Consistent to Gregor and Gruber (2021), the individual bottle observations were provided to the neural network (as the target), and the coincident temperature, salinity, and the WOA phosphate and silicate (WOA nutrients extracted from the monthly 1 degree climatology and linear interpolated to the spatial location). This parameter combination was consistent to Gregor and Gruber (2021), and testing indicated from the quality assessment this was the optimal parameter choice. For the mapping to a monthly 1 degree global grid, the CCI-SST, CCI+CMEMS SSS and WOA phosphate and silicate (for the WOA nutrients monthly climatologies) were used. The selection of CCI-SST and CMEMS SSS ensures that the TA fields are produced to the same SST and SSS as the fCO2 (sw), and therefore consistency in the carbonate system. In 2026-1 we also use the probability based SOM approach for the TA mapping as descirbed in the fCO2 (sw) section. Calculation of full surface ocean carbonate system The remaining components of the carbonate system (i.e DIC, pH etc) were calculated from fCO2 (sw) and TA using pyCO2SYS (v1.8.3.3) (Humphreys et al., 2022, 2024). The calculation also requires SST, SSS, phosphate and silicate, where the same temperature, salinity and nutrient datasets were used (as used in the neural network stages) to consistently calculate the carbonate system. pH was calculated on the total scale. The dissociation constants of Lueker et al. (2000), bisulfate dissociation constants of Dickson (1990) and total boron-salinity relationship of Uppström (1974) were used as recommended in Orr et al. (2015) and Raimondi et al. (2019) (and are the default sets used in pyCO2sys). The surface ocean carbonate system was therefore considered representative of ~0.2 m water depth. Uncertainties due to the fCO2 (sw), TA, SST, SSS, phosphate and silicate were propaged through the caluclations providing a uncertainty due to each component and a total uncertainity. In v2026-1, we also add an uncertainty component due to the dissociation constants as provided in Orr et al. (2018). Calculation of air-sea CO2 fluxes The air-sea CO2 fluxes (F) were calculated, such that vertical temperature gradients can be accounted for (Dong et al., 2022, 2024; Ford, Shutler, et al., 2024; Shutler et al., 2020; Watson et al., 2020; Woolf et al., 2016, 2019) as described in detail by Woolf et al. (2016), using FluxEngine v4.2.0 (Holding et al., 2019; Shutler et al., 2016). The CO2 flux takes the form: F = K600 (Sc / 600)-0.5 (αsubskin fCO2(sw, subskin) – αskin fCO2(atm)) (1-ice) where K600 is the gas transfer coefficient estimated using the Nightingale et al. (2000) parameterisation and wind speeds from the CCMP (v3.1) (Mears et al., 2022; Remote Sensing Systems et al., 2022). Sc is the Schmidt number estimated using the calculation in Wanninkhof et al. (2014) and the ocean’s skin temperature. α is the solubility of CO2 at the respective subskin or skin temperature and salinities which was estimated as in Weiss (1974). fCO2 (atm) and fCO2 (sw,subskin) are the fugacity of CO2 in the atmosphere and the seawater subskin layer respectively. The CCI-SST and CCI+CMEMS SSS are considered representative of the subskin temperature and salinities and used in the calculation of αsubskin. For the atmospheric side, the ocean’s skin temperature was estimated from the CCI-SST with a cool skin deviation calculated with NOAA-COARE3.6 (Edson et al., 2013; Fairall et al., 1996) using CCMP wind speed, CCI-SST and ERA5 fields as inputs. Skin salinity was calculated assuming a +0.1 psu change from the CCI+CMEMS SSS (i.e a salty skin) as in Watson et al. (2020) and Woolf et al. (2019). fCO2 (atm) was calculated using NOAA-GML atmospheric dry mixing ratio of CO2 (xCO2 (atm); Lan et al., 2023), the skin temperature and ERA5 atmospheric pressure following Dickson et al. (2009). Sea ice concentrations from the OSISAF dataset (OSI SAF, 2022) were used for the ice component. Variables All variables are provided in a single netCDF file, that has been zipped to reduce file sizes with a filename: Fordetal_UExP-FNN-U_surface-carbonate-system_vXXXX-X.nc. XXXX-X refers to the version number. Variable Units Description alpha mol m-3 uatm-1 Solubility of CO2 in seawater alpha_skin mol m-3 uatm-1 Skin solubilty of CO2 in seawater area m2 Total surface area of each 1 degree region dic μmol kg-1 Dissolved Inorganic Carbon fco2 μatm Fugacity of CO2 in seawater flux g C m-2 d-1 Air-sea CO2 flux (+ve indicates outgassing) ice unitless Sea ice concentration kw cm hr-1 Gas transfer velocity mask_sfc unitless Proportion of ocean in each 1 degree region pH unitless pH on the total scale (i.e [H+] + [HSO4-]) pH_free unitless pH on the free scale (i.e [H+]) saturation_aragonite unitless Aragonite Saturation State skin_salinity psu Skin Salinity skin_temperature ºC Skin Temperature subskin_salinity psu Subskin Salinity subskin_temperature ºC Subskin Temperature ta μmol kg-1 Total Alkalinity wind_speed m s-1 Wind speed wind_speed_second_moment m2 s-2 Second moment of wind speed Each variable contains an uncertainty estimate that follows the BIPM (2008) principles, comprising of multiple components and then a total uncertainty. We refer the user to the netCDF file for available uncertainties, but in most cases the total uncertainty is the required component. description: The Global Dam Landsat (GDL) is a publicly available dataset developed for training and evaluating deep learning models for multispectral image generation and dam construction analysis. Since no public dataset previously provided paired multispectral images acquired before dam construction and after the first reservoir impoundment together with corresponding Dam-Reservoir (DR) masks, GDL was created to address this gap. The dataset was generated using information from the Global Dam Watch (GDW) database, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 imagery (Landsat 4–9), Google Earth Engine (GEE), OpenStreetMap, the GLC_FCS30D and Dynamic World land-cover datasets, and a newly developed Detection of Initial Reservoir Impoundment (DIRI) algorithm. DIRI estimates the first reservoir impoundment year by analyzing long-term surface water dynamics within the reservoir extent. Each sample contains: 1. A six-band multispectral Landsat image acquired before dam construction. 2. A corresponding six-band multispectral image acquired after the first reservoir impoundment. 3. A DR mask indicating the dam crest, reservoir area, and background. All images have a spatial size of 512 × 512 pixels (covering 15.36 × 15.36 km²) and include the Red, Green, Blue, NIR, SWIR1, and SWIR2 bands normalized to the range [0, 1]. The DR masks were generated using NDWI-based water extraction and land-cover information, followed by manual refinement to ensure accurate reservoir and dam crest boundaries. After quality control and manual verification, the final dataset contains 2,734 samples. GDL is intended for research on remote sensing image generation, conditional generative models, dam and reservoir monitoring, environmental monitoring and management, assessment of the potential environmental and socioeconomic impacts of dam construction, analysis of hydrological and land-cover changes, and the evaluation and comparison of alternative dam development scenarios. By providing spatially explicit information on changes associated with dam construction, the dataset can also support evidence-based decision-making, infrastructure planning, and the assessment of alternative project designs and reservoir configurations.
keywords: Deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Machine Learning; Computer Vision; Dam Satellite Imagery

description: This record provides pre-event digital elevation model (DEM) composites for the area affected by the 2026-08-26 ice-rock avalanche on the north flank of Langtang Lirung, Rasuwa District, Nepal, and its downstream flood along the Chhochen Khola, Lhende Khola, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The composites are the pre-event reference surface for the post-event DEMs of this event (Shean, 2026a; Shean and Bhushan, 2026a, 2026b). The composites combine 109 EarthDEM strip DEMs, version 4.1 (Porter et al., 2024), from WorldView-1/2/3 and GeoEye-1 in-track stereo images acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. Each strip was co-registered by translation on stable ground, and the co-registered stack was tied to ICESat-2. Two sets are provided. The 2 m set is clipped to the affected corridor and has 1032 km2 of valid data. The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source, runout and upper corridor, with 1721 km2 of valid data. Both sets include median and weighted-mean DEMs, per-pixel strip count and normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD), hillshades, an ordered temporal layer set and a strip footprint index. The ordered layers are earliest- and latest-strip-on-top DEMs with source-strip and acquisition-date maps, their elevation difference and the apparent rate. No individual strip DEMs and no source imagery are distributed. All products are cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs in EPSG:32645 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 45N) with heights above the WGS 84 ellipsoid. License: CC BY-NC 4.0. DEMs provided by the Polar Geospatial Center under NSF-OPP awards 1043681, 1559691, 1542736, 1810976, and 2129685. Original Level-1B Imagery © 2009-2024 Vantor. 1. Products Nodata is -9999 in elevation, date, change, NMAD and count layers, 0 in hillshade layers and -1 in index layers. NMAD layers are nodata where fewer than two strips overlap. 00_*.png files are quick-look figures. 1.1 Corridor 2 m composite (earthdem_corridor_2m.zip: earthdem_corridor_2m_<layer>_v1.0.tif) The 2 m set is clipped to the affected-corridor polygon plus a 500 m buffer, and the strips were clipped before compositing. The 88 contributing strips were acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. The median of date_median is about 2016.7, and the median of date_wmean is about 2017.5. layer description wmean weighted-mean composite DEM (edge-distance weights) -- recommended surface for relief and as a co-registration reference median per-pixel median DEM count, nmad per-pixel strip count and NMAD (m) wmean_hs, median_hs multidirectional hillshades first, last earliest- and latest-strip-on-top DEMs, with first_hs, last_hs index_first, index_last index of the strip supplying each first / last pixel, into earthdem_corridor_2m_strip_order_v1.0.csv (0 = oldest) date_first, date_last, dt_yr acquisition date (decimal year) of the first / last pixel, and dt_yr = date_last minus date_first (decimal years) date_median, date_wmean acquisition date of the strip nearest the median value, and the weight-averaged acquisition date of the wmean dh_m elevation difference last minus first (m), where the two dates differ dhdt_myr apparent rate dh_m / dt_yr (m/yr), only where dt_yr is at least 2 years Also in the zip: earthdem_corridor_2m_strip_order_v1.0.csv: the strips in the product, oldest first. earthdem_strip_index_v1.geojson: footprints, acquisition dates and co-registration shifts of the 224 strips considered. in_mosaic marks the 208 strips in the co-registered stack. The shifts exclude the common tie to ICESat-2 (dE +0.07 m, dN -2.44 m, dU -0.10 m) that was applied to every strip. earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_stats_v1.0.json: coverage and stable-ground statistics of dh_m and dhdt_myr. 00_earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_qa_v1.0.png: quick-look figure of the ordered layers. 1.2 Source-rectangle 8 m composite (earthdem_source_8m.zip: earthdem_source_8m_<layer>_v1.0.tif) The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source area, runout and upper corridor, and is not clipped to the corridor. The rectangle is the same as in the companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c). The 8 m composite combines 66 co-registered strips acquired 2012-01-15 to 2023-12-02. The median of date_median is about 2016.0, and the median of date_wmean is about 2016.5. The layers and sidecar files are the same as in the 2 m set (section 1.1). In this set the wmean has smoother relief across strip boundaries, and the median has a slightly lower NMAD against ICESat-2 (0.90 m vs 0.94 m). 1.3 Validation (validation_v1.0.zip) The validation zip holds the ICESat-2 comparison for each DEM: a summary table, and a figure and a statistics file per product (section 3). 2. Methods Each strip was co-registered by translation in three passes. The first pass used the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM (European Space Agency and Airbus, 2022), converted to ellipsoid heights, as the reference. The second and third passes used the median of the aligned stack. Each pass solved the horizontal offset with the method of Nuth and Kääb (2011) on exposed stable ground with slopes of 1-45 degrees. Stable ground is the ESA WorldCover 2021 bare, grass, shrub, moss and cropland classes, excluding Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) 6.0 glaciers with a 100 m buffer. Before each solve, differences more than 100 m from the median difference and outliers beyond 3 NMAD were removed. The vertical offset is the median residual on stable ground. A refit was accepted only where it reduced the residual aspect signature. The strips were composited with the NASA Ames Stereo Pipeline dem_mosaic tool (Beyer et al., 2018). SETSM (Noh and Howat, 2015) is the EarthDEM stereo software. The 2 m composites use only stereo-matched pixels. Pixels that SETSM interpolated were masked along with the strip bitmask, and they are about 2 % of the valid strip area. The 8 m composites apply the bitmask only. GLO-30 was used only as the first-pass registration reference. No GLO-30 values enter any product, and voids are left as nodata. Before compositing, obvious blunders of up to hundreds of meters were removed from the strips over the source area. The 2019 Pléiades DEM (Berthier, 2026) and other independent DEMs served as the reference there. Coordinates are ITRF2020 at epoch 2022.27, the median date of the ICESat-2 data. The composite surfaces mostly date from about 2016, and plate motion of about 4 cm/yr toward the northeast moves the area about 0.25 m between 2016 and 2022. The 2015-04-25 Gorkha earthquake displaced the area by about 1.5 m horizontally, partway through the strip archive. Each strip was co-registered separately, so strips from before and after the earthquake are aligned to the same stack median. 3. Accuracy The ICESat-2 reference elevations are 10 m segment fits to all ATL03 photons, limited to exposed stable terrain. Against these segments, the four DEMs have median differences of -0.02 to +0.02 m and NMAD of 0.81 to 0.94 m. The 2 m DEMs overlap 43,031 segments and the 8 m DEMs overlap 72,773. Per-product statistics and figures are in validation_v1.0.zip. The figures include a diagnostic Nuth and Kääb (2011) horizontal fit. 4. Known issues The DEMs have voids on snow, shadow and glacier surfaces. median and wmean combine strips acquired 2009-2024, so on glacier, snow and vegetated surfaces they do not represent a single date; date_median and date_wmean give the approximate date of each pixel. first and last take each pixel from a single strip, identified in index_first / index_last and dated in date_first / date_last. The first and last mosaics can have larger errors and more blunders than median and wmean. The latest strip is from 2024-01-05. Along the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi, differences against post-event DEMs include changes from the separate 2025-07-08 Lhende Khola flood as well as the 2026-08-26 event. Blunders were removed only over the source area, inside the 2019 Pléiades footprint (section 2). Elsewhere, isolated blunders can remain where few strips overlap. Check the count and nmad layers before interpreting a large elevation change. The companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c) is co-registered to the same frame; the 8 m medians of the two records agree on stable ground to 0.8 m NMAD. 5. Research data and analysis code supporting the manuscript: “Spatial counterfactual geometry shapes coal-mine impact assessments” This repository contains the derived mine-level datasets, matching outputs, satellite extraction outputs, footprint-geometry sensitivity analyses, formal geometry tests, biomass analyses, recovery-chronology analyses, Earth Engine scripts, statistical analysis code, data dictionaries and provenance documentation used to produce the reported results. The study evaluates how spatial counterfactual geometry affects satellite-derived environmental contrasts between matched surface and underground coal mines. The primary outcomes are land-surface temperature (LST), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and woody above-ground biomass (AGB). The repository includes the complete reproducibility archive corresponding to version 1.0.0 of the analysis. Source datasets are third-party resources and remain subject to their original provider terms. These include the Global Coal Mine Tracker, Landsat Collection 2, GLC_FCS30D and the ESA Climate Change Initiative Biomass product. This repository is intended to support reproducibility, peer review and subsequent reuse of the derived analysis materials.

Raw and processed sensor, weather, and satellite datasets, plus trained model weights, from the AquaEdge project — estimating root-zone soil moisture/temperature at four depths (S1T-S4T) for agricultural fields in Morocco by fusing Pycno in-situ soil probes, Open-Meteo/ERA5 weather, Sentinel-1/2 satellite imagery, and SoilGrids soil texture. Files are grouped as zip archives by project version/model set (see the file list); each zip's internal paths mirror the folder layout documented in the companion GitHub repository's README. Companion code, notebooks, and pipelines are at the linked GitHub repository.

=========================== Introduction On 5 August 2025, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Dharali and Harshil valleys of Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, India We provide here pre-event and post-even Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of this area from Pléiades stereo-pairs acquired on the 7 October 2017 and 15 October 2025. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and the CIEST² initiative from CNES/Formaterre (https://www.poleterresolide.fr/ciest-2-nouvelle-generation-2/). We share here the Pléiades DEMs and the elevation change maps derived from these images. The collection includes: A pre-event DEM and a preview 2017-10-07_SGM_4m_align.tif A post-event DEM and a preview 2025-10-15_SGM_4m_align.tif One grid of elevation change from 2017 to 2025 and a preview 2025-10-15_SGM_4m_align-2017-10-07_SGM_4m_align_dh_after_correction.tif =========================== Methods The Pléiades stereo-images were processed using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding a DEM in 4x4 m GSD. The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then interpolated using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020) DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean’s dem_align implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). The elevation change grid is calculated using the method of the Pléiades Glacier Observatory (Berthier et al., 2024) Berthier, E., Lebreton, J., Fontannaz, D., Hosford, S., Belart, J. This dataset contains the supporting tables for the manuscript: "Uranium Comminution Ages as a Denudation Chronometer in Tectonically Active Orogens" It contains: 1. Supplementary Note S1 – Methodology Detailed description of the sequential leaching protocol for detrital uranium isolation, total digestion and uranium purification, MC‑ICP‑MS measurement procedures, determination of the α‑recoil loss fraction (fα), and construction of the flux‑weighted effective initial ratio (A0), including piecewise‑linear integration and Excel implementation. 2. Supplementary Note S2 – Supporting tables Contains two tables: Table 1 Sample details, comminution ages, and denudation rates for detrital sediments from the Asahan and Batang Toru rivers (Sumatra). Comminution ages were calculated under the conventional secular-equilibrium assumption (A₀ = 1) and with the flux-weighted effective initial ratio (A₀ᵉᶠᶠ). Denudation rates were derived via the steady-state relation ε = h/ tcom using SoilGrids regolith thicknesses. Table 2 Global comparison of uranium-series comminution-age-derived denudation rates with independent in-situ ¹⁰Be denudation rates. For each catchment, the comminution age is calculated first under the conventional A₀ = 1 assumption, and then with a representative non-equilibrium A₀ (0.98–0.99), consistent with the bedrock ²³⁴U depletion observed in active orogens. The ¹⁰Be denudation rate serves as the independent reference.

CitiesGOER is a database that provides environmental data for 52,602 cities and 48 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 2 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927. Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species. Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914. CitiesGOER was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. The identities and coordinates of cities were sourced from a data set with information for cities with a population size larger than 1000 that was created by Opendatasoft and made available from https://public.opendatasoft.com/explore/dataset/geonames-all-cities-with-a-population-1000/table/?disjunctive.cou_name_en&sort=name. The data was downloaded on 22-JULY-2023 and afterwards filtered for cities with a population of 5000 or above. Cities where information on the country was missing were removed. The coordinates of cities were used to extract the environmental data via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.6-47) in the R 4.2.1 environment. Version 2023.08 provided median values from 23 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 and from 18 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0, both for the 2050s (2041-2060). Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1). Version 2023.09 used similar methods as for previous versions to provide median values from 13 GCMs for the 2090s (2081-2100) for SSP 5-8.5. The locations of the 52,602 cities are mapped in one of the series available from the TreeGOER Global Zones atlas that can be obtained from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8252756. Version 2024.10 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Holdridge Life Zones. Information is given for historical (1901-1920), contemporary (1979-2013) and future (2061-2080; separately for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) climates inferred from global raster layers that are available for download from DRYAD and were created for the following article: Elsen et al. 2022. Accelerated shifts in terrestrial life zones under rapid climate change. Global Change Biology, 28, 918–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15962. Version 2024.10 further includes Holdridge Life Zones for the climates that were available from the previous versions, calculating biotemperatures and life zones with similar methods as used by Holdridge (1947; 1967) and Elsen et al. (2022) (for future climates, median values were determined first for monthly maximum and minimum temperatures across GCMs ). The distributions of the 48,129 species documented in TreeGOER across the Holdridge Life Zones are given in this Zenodo archive: https://zenodo.org/records/14020914. Version 2024.11 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Köppen-Geiger climate zones. Information is given for historical (1901-1930, 1931-1960, 1961-1990) and future (2041-2070 and 2071-2099) climates, with for the future climates seven scenarios each (SSP 1-1.9, SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 3-7.0, SSP 4-3.4, SSP 4-6.0 and SSP 5-8.5). This data set was created from 30 arc-second raster layers available via: Beck, H.E., McVicar, T.R., Vergopolan, N. et al. High-resolution (1 km) Köppen-Geiger maps for 1901–2099 based on constrained CMIP6 projections. Sci Data 10, 724 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02549-6 Version 2025.03 includes extra columns for the baseline, 2050s and 2090s datasets that partially correspond to climate zones used in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database. One of these zones are the Whittaker biome types, available as a polygon from the plotbiomes package (see also here). Whittaker biome types were extracted with similar R scripts as described by Kindt 2025 (these were also used to calculate environmental ranges of TreeGOER species, as archived here). Version 2025.03 further includes information for the baseline climate on the steady state water table depth, obtained from a 30 arc-seconds raster layer calculated by the GLOBGM v1.0 model (Verkaik et al. 2024). Also included was the elevation, obtained from the same WorldClim 2.1 raster layer used to prepare TreeGOER. Version 2026.04 includes a new Excel workbook that provides the nearest urban centre centroid from the Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database (UCDB R2024A, reference epoch 2025, World Mollweide, EPSG:54009, 1km; https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/datasets.php ; Melchiori et al. 2024). Different searches were done for the nearest urban centre centroid, searching among all centres, among all centres with a 2025 population size ≥ 100,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 500,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 1 million, among all centres with a population size ≥ 5 million and among all centres with a population size ≥ 10 million. Distances between city locations from CitiesGOER and urban centre centroids were calculated in R via geosphere::distGeo (version 1.5-20; Hijmans 2024). Version 2026.09 includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_GAIPED) that provide the locations of cities in Climatic Moisture Index zones (https://zenodo.org/records/21808912) calculated via the Potential Evapotranspiration (ET0) obtained from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database (GAIPED; Zomer et al. 2022). Version 2026.09 also includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_Global Climate Zones_Audebert) that provides the locations of cities in Global Climate Zones derived via the Mean Annual Biotemperature and the Inverted Aridity Index (https://zenodo.org/records/21901225), using the decision framework developed by Audebert et al. (2026). As an alternative to CitiesGOER, the ClimateForecasts database (https://zenodo.org/records/10776414) documents the environmental conditions at the locations of 15,504 weather stations. ClimateForecasts was integrated in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (see Kindt et al. 2023). When using CitiesGOER in your work, cite this depository and the following: Fick, S. E., & Hijmans, R. description: This Zenodo record contains the analysis-ready data and Python scripts supporting the manuscript "Physiological costs of drought resistance shape vegetation recovery". The study examines the relationships between the physiological costs of drought resistance and vegetation recovery using satellite observations, meteorological datasets, and FLUXNET measurements during 2018-2023. The deposited data include event-level and model-ready tables for the main analysis, the alternative-meteorology analysis, and the FLUXNET site-level evaluation. The deposited code contains the Python scripts used for the analyses and figure generation reported in the manuscript. The original TROPOSIF, MODIS LAI, ERA5-Land, GLEAM, MERRA-2, and FLUXNET datasets are not redistributed in this record and should be obtained from the original providers identified in the manuscript’s Data availability statement.

ClimateForecasts is a database that provides environmental data for 15,504 weather station locations and 49 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 3 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927. Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species. Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914. A similar extraction process was used for the CitiesGOER database that is also available from Zenodo via https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.8175429. ClimateForecasts (as the CitiesGOER) was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023) or EcoregionsTreeFinder (Kindt & Pedercini 2025) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. One example of combining data from these different sets in the R statistical environment is available from this Rpub: https://rpubs.com/Roeland-KINDT/1114902. The identities including the geographical coordinates of weather stations were sourced from Meteostat, specifically by downloading (17-FEB-2024) the ‘lite dump’ data set with information for active weather stations only. Two weather stations where the country could not be determined from the ISO 3166-1 code of ‘XA’ were removed. If weather stations had the same name, but occurred in different ISO 3166-2 regions, this region code was added to the name of the weather station between square brackets. Afterwards duplicates (weather stations of the same name and region) were manually removed. Bioclimatic variables for future climates correspond to the median values from 24 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 for the 2050s (2041-2060), from 21 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0 for the 2050s and from 13 GCMs for SSP 5-8.5 for the 2090s. Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1). Maps were added in version 2024.03 where locations of weather stations were shown on a map of the Climatic Moisture Index (CMI). These maps were created by a similar process as in the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas from the environmental raster layers used to create the TreeGOER via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.7-46) in the R 4.2.1 environment. Added country boundaries were obtained from Natural Earth as Admin 0 – countries vector layers (version 5.1.1). Also added after obtaining them from Natural Earth were Admin 0 – Breakaway, Disputed areas (version 5.1.0, coloured yellow in the atlas) and Roads (version 5.0.0, coloured red in the atlas). For countries where the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database included subnational levels, boundaries were added and depicted as dot-dash lines. These subnational levels correspond to level 3 boundaries in the World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions. These were obtained from https://github.com/tdwg/wgsrpd. Check Brummit 2001 for details such as the maps shown at the end of this document. Maps for version 2024.07 modified the dimensions of the sheets to those used in version 2024.06 of the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas. Another modification was the inclusion of Natural Earth boundaries for Lakes (version 5.0.0, coloured darkblue in the atlas). description: The Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset provides estimates of annual sediment volume and reservoir sedimentation rate (RSR) for 34,372 reservoirs worldwide. The dataset was developed using the Integrated Reservoir Sedimentation Prediction (IRSP) framework, which integrates machine learning with climatic, geomorphic, hydrological, and reservoir-specific predictors. For each reservoir, the dataset provides the predicted annual sediment volume, its prediction variability quantified by the standard deviation (SD) across spatial cross-validation folds, and the RSR, defined as the ratio of annual sediment volume to initial reservoir storage capacity. Each reservoir is linked to the Global Dam Watch (GDW) v1.0 dataset through its corresponding GDW identifier.

README This repository contains the processed datasets and R scripts supporting the manuscript entitled “Asymmetric impacts of supply- and demand-driven flash droughts on leaf senescence.” The study investigates the asymmetric effects of supply-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with precipitation deficits, and demand-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with enhanced atmospheric evaporative demand, on vegetation leaf senescence across the Northern Hemisphere during 2001–2024. The repository contains the processed datasets supporting the analyses and visualizations. Owing to repository file-size constraints, some processed datasets are provided as ZIP archives. Compression does not alter the data content, and the files should be extracted before use. Phenology_North_poly.csv contains annual satellite-derived vegetation phenological metrics for each grid cell across the Northern Hemisphere and was used for phenological quality control and anomaly calculation. all_GS_FD_years.csv contains the grid-year combinations with at least one FD overlapping the growing season and was used to identify non-FD years for calculating the phenological baseline. dEOS_poly.csv contains the resulting LSD anomalies derived from the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). The term “EOS” used in the file name and scripts denotes the end-of-season phenological metric and corresponds to the leaf senescence date (LSD) used in the manuscript. phenology_poly_pentad.csv records the long-term mean timing of the start, peak, and end of the growing season, expressed as the corresponding 8-day periods for each grid cell. SMrz_drought_events.csv contains the flash drought events identified from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles using 01_FD_detection.R, including the original P1–P4 event timing indices, minimum soil-moisture percentile, onset rate, and cumulative severity. SMrz_drought_events_mean_environment_anomaly.csv contains flash drought events overlapping the growing season and their mean environmental anomalies calculated over the complete, untruncated P1–P4 event periods. These variables were used to characterize the hydroclimatic conditions of the events and as inputs for their subsequent classification into supply- and demand-driven flash droughts. final_FD_events.csv is the final analytical dataset and contains 1,141,551 event records. It retains the original, untruncated P1–P4 indices and was constructed by (1) retaining FD events that overlapped the growing season, (2) retaining phenological observations within the grid-specific median ± 2.5 median absolute deviations and grid cells with an interannual LSD standard deviation below 30 days, (3) retaining only grid-year combinations with a single FD overlapping the growing season, and (4) excluding non-target land-cover and biome classes, including croplands, and records with predictor values outside their respective 1st–99th percentile ranges. This dataset was used in the subsequent LSD-response, structural equation modeling, random forest, SHAP, and model-improvement analyses. Meanenv_EarlyGS_anomaly.csv and Meanenv_LateGS_anomaly.csv contain environmental anomalies during the early and late growing seasons, respectively, while Additional_data.csv provides the additional background and vegetation variables used to construct the predictor set for the RF, SHAP, and related analyses. The background spatial datasets include MODIS_IGBP0.1deg_type.csv, which contains MODIS International Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land-cover classifications at a spatial resolution of 0.1°; phe_poly_biome.csv, which contains biome classifications based on the World Wildlife Fund terrestrial ecoregions; and Background_MAP.csv and Background_MAT.csv, which contain mean annual precipitation and mean annual temperature, respectively. worldmap.zip contains the world map and national boundary files used for spatial visualization. The datasets supporting the response and modeling analyses include dEOSsig_supply_poly.csv and dEOSsig_demand_poly.csv, which contain the statistical significance of LSD responses to supply- and demand-driven flash droughts, respectively. RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_EVI.csv and RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_SIF.csv contain the random forest model outputs used to evaluate and compare the simulated LSD responses based on EVI and SIF. FD_ET_series.csv contains the time series of evapotranspiration anomalies before and after flash drought onset. The SHAP outputs from the random forest models are provided in shap_mat_EVI_demand.rds, shap_mat_SIF_demand.rds, shap_mat_EVI_supply.rds, and shap_mat_SIF_supply.rds. These files contain the SHAP values used to quantify and visualize the contributions of climatic, biological, and flash-drought-related variables to the modeled LSD responses under the two flash drought types. The accompanying R scripts perform the principal data processing, statistical analyses, and visualization procedures used in the study. 01_FD_detection.R identifies flash drought events from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles, calculates their characteristics, and applies the prescribed duration criterion of 4–12 consecutive 8-day periods. 02_phenology_extraction.R extracts vegetation phenological metrics from satellite-derived EVI and SIF time series. 03_FD_environment_anomaly.R retains FD events that overlap the growing season without modifying their original P1–P4 indices and calculates environmental anomalies over their complete event periods. 04_phenology_anomaly_nonFD_baseline.R calculates phenological anomalies relative to years without growing-season FDs and applies the grid-specific phenological quality-control and single-event grid-year criteria. 05_final_FD_event_filtering.R generates the final analytical dataset from the records processed in the preceding steps and applies the land-cover, biome, and predictor percentile filters. 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R conducts random forest modeling and SHAP analysis to identify the climatic and biotic controls of leaf senescence responses. 07_SEM_analysis.R performs structural equation modeling to examine the pathways through which the two flash drought types regulate leaf senescence. 08_phenology_response_significance.R evaluates the significance of phenological responses to flash droughts. 09_visualization_analysis.R generates the principal figures and statistical visualizations, and 10_visualization_SHAP_analysis.R produces the SHAP importance and dependence plots. The original satellite, reanalysis, and ancillary datasets are not redistributed in this repository, except for the processed background and boundary data used for visualization. The original root-zone soil-moisture percentile series and processed LAI time series are not redistributed because of their large file sizes; their data sources and processing procedures are documented in the manuscript and accompanying code. The original datasets are publicly available from their respective data providers, as documented in the associated manuscript. The deposited processed datasets and scripts provide the materials needed to evaluate the reported results and reproduce the principal analyses and visualizations. Code execution and software environment All scripts were developed and tested using R version 4.5.2 in RStudio under Windows. No GPU or other non-standard hardware is required for most analyses. Before running the scripts, users should replace the placeholder input, output, and figure paths at the beginning of each script with valid local paths. The scripts can then be executed directly in RStudio. The scripts are numbered according to their recommended execution order. Scripts 01_FD_detection.R–05_final_FD_event_filtering.R perform FD detection, phenological extraction, anomaly calculation, and construction of the final analytical dataset. Scripts 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R–08_phenology_response_significance.R perform the RF–SHAP, SEM, and significance analyses, respectively. The final visualization scripts generate the figures reported in the manuscript. The deposited processed datasets allow the principal statistical analyses and figures to be reproduced without rerunning the complete processing chain from the original satellite and reanalysis data. Using the prepared input datasets, all scripts except 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R typically complete within several minutes, although runtime depends on computer performance and data-transfer speed. The complete random forest and SHAP workflow in 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R was run on a multicore server and required approximately four days. This script calculates one response–FD-type SHAP combination per run and should be executed for the four combinations of EVI/SIF and supply-/demand-driven FDs to regenerate all deposited SHAP objects. The principal R packages and tested versions were: data.table 1.17.8, dplyr 1.1.4, zoo 1.8-12, doSNOW 1.0.20, foreach 1.5.2, ranger 0.17.0, ggplot2 4.0.0, patchwork 1.3.2, RColorBrewer 1.1-3, usdm 2.1-7, ALEPlot 1.1, mlbench 2.1-6, fastshap 0.1.1, future 1.33.2, lavaan 0.6-17, raster 3.6-26, terra 1.7-78, sf 1.0-23, plyr 1.8.9, and scales 1.4.0. A complete README file and R session record will be included with the code archive in the next repository version.

description: This dataset is for “Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan” by Wei et al. in Atmospheric Environment. The contents are described in the sheet “Readme” of the Excel file named “Dataset_cw260904.xlsx”. The dataset contains the data used in the manuscript, including average fluorescence spectra, fluorescence indices, atmospheric fluorescence volumes, normalized fluorescence volumes, and PARAFAC components of water-soluble organic matter (WSOM) in atmospheric aerosol samples collected at forest, remote, and urban sites in Japan. The dataset also includes the correlations of the atmospheric fluorescence volumes of the PARAFAC components with the concentrations of water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) and meteorological parameters. The dataset further provides fluorescence indices and atmospheric fluorescence volumes for three subfractions of WSOM obtained from aerosol and rainwater samples collected in Nagoya. The excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectra of WSOM in aqueous extracts were measured using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (FP-6600, JASCO) with a 1-cm path length quartz cell. The ranges of the excitation and emission wavelengths were 235-500 nm and 300-600 nm, respectively. The drEEM toolbox for MATLAB was used to preprocess the EEMs and to perform parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis. The concentrations of WSOC and water-soluble inorganic ions were measured using a total organic carbon analyzer and ion chromatography, respectively. The dataset was obtained in the study conducted under JSPS KAKENHI (JP26281007, JP23H00515, and JP19KK0265); ArCS II (JPMXD1420318865); and ERDF from ERCA (JPMEERF20232001). Other acknowledgments are provided in the associated manuscript.

Derived datasets underlying Ismail and Yamashiki, "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins", submitted to Earth Systems and Environment. The study assesses fluvial flood hazard and population exposure across Pakistan's five major drainage basins (872,782 km², 99% of national territory) from the 50-year to the 500-year return period, combining Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) inundation mapping with GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge, Generalised Extreme Value flood frequency analysis, and hydraulic-geometry depth estimation. A first-order sensitivity decomposition attributes total exposure uncertainty to four sources: rating curve parameters, DEM resolution, GEV parameter uncertainty and population data uncertainty. CONTENTS Derived datasets (14 CSV files) AMS_5basins.csv annual maximum series, five basins, 1979-2025 GEV_parameters_47yr.csv fitted GEV location, scale and shape parameters gev_shape_intervals.csv 95% intervals on the shape parameter GEV_return_levels_47yr.csv return levels, T50 to T500 prep_design_discharges.csv design discharges by basin and return period prep_depths.csv design depths from the generalised rating curve prep_depth_agreement.csv depth agreement across rating curve formulations prep_exposure_90m.csv population and built-up exposure, 90 m framework prep_exposure_southern_30m.csv Southern Basin exposure at 30 m prep_exposure_ranges.csv exposure ranges and range factors by basin prep_national_totals.csv national exposure totals prep_uncertainty_decomposition.csv four-source sensitivity decomposition prep_central_bayes.csv Central Basin Bayesian GEV estimates prior_sensitivity_grid.csv prior sensitivity for the Bayesian fit Published tables (22 CSV files) Every table in the paper as a separate file: the five main tables (Table1-Table5) and all seventeen supplementary table parts (TableS1-TableS14, including the a/b splits of S5, S6 and S12), exactly as published. Every number reported in the paper can be checked directly against these files. NOT INCLUDED Input rasters and gauge records are third-party data distributed under their own terms and are not redistributed here. Their sources and versions are listed in the paper's Data Availability statement: GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge v4.0 (Copernicus Climate Change Service); SRTM 30 m and 90 m (NASA Earthdata, USGS EarthExplorer); GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT-S R2023A epoch 2025 (European Commission JRC); HydroBASINS Level 4 (HydroSHEDS); Sentinel-1 GRD (Copernicus, via Google Earth Engine); Global Flood Database 2010 extent. Gauge records are available from the Global Runoff Data Centre, Koblenz, on request under their data-sharing policy and are not redistributable. Analysis code is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. CHANGES FROM VERSION 1.0 Version 1.0 (April 2026) accompanied the originally submitted manuscript. This version corresponds to the revised manuscript and supersedes it. The sensitivity decomposition has been recomputed: the population uncertainty term now uses the full width of the symmetric ±30% bound on gridded population counts, as set out in Section 3.7 of the revised paper. Shape-parameter confidence intervals, design depths, Southern Basin dual-resolution exposure and the full set of published tables have been added.
