description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height: Surface elevation wnd100m: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth: Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness: Surface roughness length influx_toa: Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo: Surface albedo temperature: Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature: Soil temperature at level 4 runoff: Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct: Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse: Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude: Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth: Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN. Source: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Terms of Use These cutouts contain processed meteorological data derived from ERA5, provided by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), and SARAH-3, provided by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 Contains modified EUMETSAT CM SAF SARAH-3 data (2026). Copyright © 2026 EUMETSAT. All intellectual property rights to the original CM SAF products belong to EUMETSAT. These products are made available free of charge under the applicable EUMETSAT data policy. Users must acknowledge EUMETSAT when using or redistributing the data and are requested to cite the original SARAH-3 dataset: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Licensing and Attribution The cutouts are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, subject to the attribution requirements associated with the original data sources. description: Overview This record contains the full dataset (data/) supporting the Research Paper titled Integrating functionally-based soil organic carbon threshold models with reconstructed historical baselines to evaluate a soil degradation boundary in India and every raw/reconstructed geospatial input, every pixel- and ecoregion-level analysis-ready table, and every precomputed intermediate result (threshold-fit curves, sensitivity and resilience classifications) used to generate the Research paper results using the code accessible openly as Jupyter-notebook analysis code on https://github.com/sirtiza34/SOC_Functional_Thresholds_India_Analysis and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22806576. Together they allow full reproduction of the Research Paper's quantitative results. All the dataset files are distributed only through this Zenodo record and the code repositories document this and points here. Spatial and temporal scope The dataset covers the soilscapes delimited by the territorial extents of India. Contemporary layers are at 250 m pixel resolution (50.48 million pixels) and temporal snapshot of 2019 developed from the SOC concentration data available at https://soilgrids.org/. The historical baseline is sourced from the Sanderman et al. (2017)’s paleo-SOC reconstructions available at https://github.com/whrc/Soil-Carbon-Debt. The baseline is reconstructed on a coarser (~10 km) grid. All analyses are synthesized to 49 terrestrial ecoregions (World Wildlife Federation) covering the territory of India, and further stratified into 1,156 ecoregion × soil-order × land-use Environmental Context Units (ECUs) for threshold assignment. Contents, by category Pixel-level analysis-ready tables (the three large files) master_analysis_database.parquet — the master contemporary pixel database, 50.48 million rows, carrying assigned functional thresholds and derived metrics for every 250 m pixel in India. step6_functional_state_sample.csv — a spatially block-declustered sample of 395,750 pixels carrying per-pixel probability of being below threshold, P(SOC<T), for each of the four response domains. step4_distance_sample.csv — a pixel sample used to compute distance-to-functional-transition. Geospatial layers (rasters and vectors) ecoregion_id.tif, accel_class_map.tif, step10_feature_stack.tif, step13_soc_stack.tif — raster layers used in mapping and feature construction. step11_map_c_class_raster.npy / step14_boundary_raster.npy (with matching *_meta.pkl files) — precomputed classification and boundary-classification rasters plus their georeferencing metadata. india_boundary.geojson — national boundary vector used for map masking/plotting. Ecoregion-level and threshold tables About 30 CSV files cover, among others, the common analytical framework and state variables per ecoregion, tiered threshold assignment and tier-usage area shares, national and per-ecoregion threshold estimates and their uncertainty, historical-depletion/functional-risk correlation by response domain, degradation-boundary classification per ecoregion, area-weighted vs. unit-weighted synthesis, directional consistency and cross-domain overlap, resilience-opportunity and continued-loss-risk groupings, degradation hotspot lists, and area-weighting tables. Precomputed model curves step12_curves.pkl, step13_curves.pkl — fitted threshold-response curve objects. Data provenance Historical SOC baseline: depth-integrated (0–30 cm) reconstruction following the global SOC-debt method of Sanderman, Hengl & Fiske (2017, PNAS). Contemporary soil properties: SoilGrids v2.0 (Poggio et al., 2021, SOIL). Ecoregion boundaries: WWF terrestrial ecoregions. File formats GeoTIFF (.tif), NumPy array (.npy) with pickled metadata (.pkl), GeoJSON (.geojson), Apache Parquet (.parquet), and CSV — all openly readable with standard open-source GIS/Python tooling (rasterio, pyarrow, pandas, geopandas).

description: This dataset provides global gridded solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) derived from TROPOMI (Sentinel-5P) observations at 0.05° spatial resolution and 8-day temporal resolution, covering the period from 1 May 2018 to 31 July 2025. The input data are ungridded (Level-2) SIF soundings retrieved using the artificial neural network (ANN) approach developed by Li et al.(10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987), which are publicly available on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/16537343). These soundings were aggregated onto a regular grid following the oversampling approach of Frankenberg et al., as implemented in SatelliteGridding.jl (https://github.com/cfranken/SatelliteGridding). The variable dcSIF denotes daily-corrected SIF, obtained by applying the day-length correction factor following Köhler et al.(https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GL079031), which scales instantaneous SIF to daily average values. Data are provided as one NetCDF file per year. Citation: If you use this dataset, please cite the original SIF retrieval paper by Li et al. (2025; 10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987), as well as the methodological references listed above where appropriate.

description: This dataset comprises 784 topsoil samples selected from the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), including soil organic carbon content, geographic coordinates, and visible–near-infrared spectral data covering 400–2400 nm at a standardized 10 nm interval. The dataset also integrates ten environmental covariates: clay content, silt content, cation exchange capacity, soil pH, elevation, slope, annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, NDVI, and land-cover type. Based on these covariates, the samples were classified into five geographical environmental zones using a Gaussian mixture model. The dataset supports comparisons between global and geographically stratified models for soil organic carbon estimation and facilitates the regional application of global soil spectral libraries.

description: This repository contains the processed datasets and R analysis scripts used to generate the figures and results in the manuscript "Lake Expansion Amid Global Aridification: Disentangling the Drivers of Qinghai Lake's Water Storage Gain." This dataset contains pixel-level urban morphology and Landsat-derived land surface temperature data for the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area, Mexico. It is organized on a 30-meter analytical grid (900 m² per cell) and includes 13 morphological predictor variables — such as green area, concrete roof area, road area, average tree height, and total trees — along with land surface temperature derived from a Landsat 9 OLI-2/TIRS-2 scene acquired on June 16, 2024. The dataset was constructed by integrating geospatial data from multiple sources: the USGS Earth Explorer (Landsat imagery), Visor Urbano Guadalajara (urban tree inventory), SITE Jalisco (green areas and water bodies), and Catastro Municipal de Guadalajara (building footprints, roads, and sidewalks).

description: Lake-Specific ERA5, ISIMIP3b and ESA CCI Lakes Datasets Overview: This repository contains lake-specific climate and lake-observation datasets extracted and processed from three established data products: - ERA5 meteorological data - ISIMIP3b climate forcing data - ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1 The datasets were extracted for four study lakes: - Lake Balaton - Lake Iseo - Lake Mälaren - Lake Wylerbergmeer The processing workflow identifies the source-data grid cells intersecting each lake, extracts the corresponding time series, and produces lake-specific NetCDF datasets suitable for subsequent analysis. **Important:** The files in this repository are derived/extracted products. They do not replace the original ERA5, ISIMIP3b, or ESA CCI Lakes datasets. Users should consult and cite the original data providers and comply with the terms and licences of the original datasets. Study lakes: | Lake | ERA5 grid cells | ISIMIP3b grid cells | ESA CCI Lakes | | Balaton | 7 | 4 | Available (ID 310) | | Iseo | 1 | 2 | Available (ID 300014185) | | Mälaren | 17 | 9 | Available (ID 163) | | Wylerbergmeer | 1 | 1 | Not available | The lake polygons for Balaton, Iseo and Mälaren were obtained from HydroLAKES. A custom shapefile was used for Wylerbergmeer. 1. ERA5 meteorological data 1.1 Grid-cell identification The ERA5 workflow identifies the ERA5 0.25° × 0.25° grid cells that intersect each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - The lake bounding box is calculated. - A regular 0.25° latitude–longitude ERA5 grid is generated over the bounding box. - Square polygons representing the ERA5 grid cells are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection is used to identify all grid cells intersecting the lake polygon. - The coordinates of the selected grid-cell centres are extracted. 1.2 ERA5 data extraction Hourly ERA5 single-level meteorological data are downloaded for each selected grid cell using the Copernicus Climate Data Store and the ecmwfr R package. The extraction period is: 1980-01-01 to 2026-05-31 The following variables are included: | Variable | ERA5 short name | Units | | 2 m air temperature | t2m | K | | 2 m dew point temperature | d2m | K | | Surface pressure | sp | Pa | | Surface solar radiation downwards | ssrd | J m⁻² | | Surface thermal radiation downwards | strd | J m⁻² | | Total precipitation | tp | m | | 10 m zonal wind component | u10 | m s⁻¹ | | 10 m meridional wind component | v10 | m s⁻¹ | | Total cloud cover | tcc | fraction (0–1) | 1.3 ERA5 merging The individual ERA5 grid-cell NetCDF files are merged into one multi-station NetCDF file per lake. The merged datasets contain: - A common time dimension (valid_time) - Station identifiers corresponding to ERA5 grid cells - Latitude and longitude for each grid cell - Meteorological variables stored as time × station arrays; - Selected metadata copied from the original ERA5 files, including units, long names and standard names. Final files: - lake_balaton_era5.nc - lake_iseo_era5.nc - lake_mälaren_era5.nc - lake_wylerbergmeer_era5.nc 2. ESA CCI Lakes products 2.1 Data source and extraction Daily ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1, are downloaded from the CEDA THREDDS server for 1992–2022. A unique ESA CCI Lakes ID is used to isolate each lake from the static lake mask. | Lake | ESA CCI Lakes ID | | Mälaren | 163 | | Balaton | 310 | | Iseo | 300014185 | | Wylerbergmeer | Not available | Wylerbergmeer is therefore excluded from the ESA CCI Lakes dataset. 2.2 Spatial processing The static CCI_lakeid mask is used to: - Identify all grid cells belonging to the selected lake ID - Calculate a bounding box around the selected pixels, with a one-pixel buffer - Extract a reduced spatial subset from the global dataset After subsetting, all variables are masked so that only pixels belonging to the selected lake ID remain valid. Other pixels are assigned _FillValue. 2.3 Variables The extracted ESA CCI Lakes variables are: | Variable | Name | Units | | Lake surface water temperature | lake_surface_water_temperature | K | | LSWT uncertainty | lswt_uncertainty | K | | Chlorophyll-a concentration | chla_mean | mg m⁻³ | | Chlorophyll-a uncertainty | chla_uncertainty | % | | Turbidity | turbidity_mean | NTU | | Turbidity uncertainty | turbidity_uncertainty | % | | Lake ice cover class | lake_ice_cover_class | categorical | | Lake surface water extent | lake_surface_water_extent | km² | | Water surface height above reference datum | water_surface_height_above_reference_datum | m | Associated quality-control variables include: lswt_quality_level, lwlr_quality_flag, lwe_quality_flag and lwl_quality_flag. 2.4 Quality control LSWT LSWT and its uncertainty are retained only for: lswt_quality_level = 4 or 5 Values equal to the specified fill value are removed, and invalid pixels are set to NA. Chlorophyll-a chla_mean and chla_uncertainty are filtered using lwlr_quality_flag. Pixels for which the relevant poor/low-consistency quality bits are set are removed. Turbidity Turbidity and its uncertainty use the same lwlr_quality_flag filtering approach as chlorophyll-a. Ice cover Only the following classes are retained: 1 = water and 2 = ice. All other values are assigned NA. Lake surface water extent Only lwe_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwe_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. Water level Only lwl_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwl_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. 2.5 Final CCI Lakes datasets After filtering, daily files are merged along a new time dimension. The final NetCDF datasets have dimensions: lat × lon × time Final files: - lake_mälaren_cci_lakes.nc - lake_balaton_cci_lakes.nc - lake_iseo_cci_lakes.nc 3. ISIMIP3b climate data 3.1 Grid-cell identification The ISIMIP3b workflow identifies the 0.5° × 0.5° grid cells intersecting each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - A regular 0.5° latitude–longitude grid is generated. - Grid-cell polygons are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection identifies the grid cells intersecting the lake. - The selected grid-cell centre coordinates are stored. 3.2 Climate models The ISIMIP3b data include the following GCMs: - GFDL-ESM4 - IPSL-CM6A-LR - MPI-ESM1-2-HR - MRI-ESM2-0 - UKESM1-0-LL 3.3 Scenarios The following scenarios are included: | Simulation | Period | | Historical | 1850–2014 | | SSP126 | 2015–2100 | | SSP370 | 2015–2100 | | SSP585 | 2015–2100 | 3.4 Variables | Variable | ISIMIP3b short name | Units | | Near-surface air temperature | tas | K | | Daily maximum air temperature | tasmax | K | | Daily minimum air temperature | tasmin | K | | Near-surface relative humidity | hurs | % | | Near-surface specific humidity | huss | kg kg⁻¹ | | Surface air pressure | ps | Pa | | Precipitation | pr | kg m⁻² s⁻¹ | | Surface downwelling shortwave radiation | rsds | W m⁻² | | Surface downwelling longwave radiation | `rlds` | W m⁻² | | Near-surface wind speed | sfcWind | m s⁻¹ | 3.5 Extraction and merging The global ISIMIP3b NetCDF files are opened and the grid cells identified for each lake are extracted. The extracted 10-year chunks are concatenated to reconstruct continuous time series for: - historical: 1850–2014 - SSP126: 2015–2100 - SSP370: 2015–2100 - SSP585: 2015–2100 The time axis is reconstructed using the same time origin across the complete period. Latitude and longitude are retained for each grid cell, and variables are assembled into time × station arrays. Selected metadata, including units, long names, standard names and selected global attributes, are copied from the original ISIMIP3b files. The final output is one multi-station NetCDF file per lake, GCM and scenario. The deposit contains three tables. gcb_panel.csv is a country–year panel with 13,327 rows covering 1990–2050: greenhouse gas emissions in CO₂e with and without LULUCF, population observed to 2019 and projected thereafter, and GDP at current and at constant 2015 prices. gcb_indicators.csv holds one row per country with every allocation indicator, the components of the re-specified ECPC, and the descriptive weights. gcb_national_budgets.csv converts each share into an allocation in GtCO₂e, into years of 2019 emissions, and into the constant annual reduction rate that exhausts it by 2050, for every combination of criterion and budget scenario. codebook.md defines every variable with its unit, time window and source, and is regenerated from the configuration file on every run, so it cannot drift from the calculation. MANIFEST.json records the SHA-256 checksum of each of the 12 source files and of each output, together with the versions of Python and of every library used. A single command, run_all.py, rebuilds everything from the frozen sources and exits with a non-zero status if the replication of the published tables fails.

description: This Zenodo record contains code and analysis data supporting a study on deep-learning-based mapping and evaluation of river barriers. The materials cover annotation-format conversion, dataset preparation, model training and inference, detection-performance evaluation, approximate barrier-size classification, and cross-basin barrier-density analysis. The repository includes scripts for converting LabelMe annotations to YOLO and COCO formats, randomly splitting a COCO dataset into training, validation, and test subsets using an 8:1:1 ratio, training YOLO11 and RT-DETRv2 models, conducting batch inference with RT-DETRv2, and evaluating predictions against manually interpreted ground-truth annotations using intersection over union (IoU). An additional script estimates approximate barrier lengths from annotated coordinates and classifies barriers into three size classes (≤30 m, 30–100 m, and >100 m). The record also includes analysis data for 58 selected sub-basins used to compare barrier counts and densities derived from three sources: manual visual interpretation, deep-learning predictions, and Global Dam Watch (GDW). These data were used for the statistical analyses reported in the associated study. The object-detection workflow includes six river-barrier classes: weir, dam, sluice, tide, earth, and lock. Some scripts retain environment-specific file paths and therefore require users to modify input/output paths before execution. RT-DETRv2 and YOLO scripts also depend on their respective external frameworks, configuration files, and model weights. Further details are provided in the accompanying README. RT-DETRv2-x-bestpt.zip contains the trained weights of the best-performing RT-DETRv2-X model used in this study. The model was selected for subsequent cross-basin generalization testing and river-barrier detection analyses.

Updated version of the 2 m merged Pléiades DEM where a ~10 m horizontal shift was corrected. =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal (Rasuwa) and Tibet : (see e.g. https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/) We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades tri-stereo acquired on the 13 October 2019, 7 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The updated collection includes one DEM : 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The three Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Shean et al., 2016, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total nine DEMs in 2x2m, 4x4m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean's demcoreg (https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/72886193) implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). Then, for each GSD (20m, 4m and 2m), the three DEMs are mosaicked using the median value. 2019-10-13_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the three above DEMs retaining the highest resolution (2 m)where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change 1. Overview This archive contains the processed data, Python scripts, reproduced figure outputs, and per-figure statistics used for the manuscript "Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change". The original daily meteorological forcing data and high-resolution process-based model outputs for 1,427,688 lakes are too large to include here. The archive instead provides processed lake-level, gridded, validation, and figure-source datasets sufficient to reproduce the main quantitative results and figures included in this package. 2. Getting Started and System Requirements 2.1 Zenodo Archives and Extraction The repository is distributed as standard ZIP archives and approximately 1 GB file parts so that large downloads can be transferred reliably: README.md: documentation for archive extraction, software setup, data contents, and reproduction. lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip: script/ and requirements.txt. lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip: demo data, external geospatial data, and processed data (including lake_qc_exclusions.csv) other than the two largest NPZ files. lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part007: parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/daily_nonoverlap_results.npz. lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part011: parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/background_results.npz. lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip: 26 reference PDF/JPG files for 13 manuscript figures and 13 per-figure statistics CSV files, regenerated in the latest test run. Demo outputs are generated separately by script/demo.py. The README, scripts, core data archive, and every part of both large data archives are required to rerun every analysis. The results archive is optional and provides reference outputs for comparison. Download all required files into one directory. Individual .partNNN files cannot be extracted directly; they must first be joined in numerical order. On macOS, open Terminal in the download directory and run: cat lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip cat lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip mkdir -p lake_thermal_structure cp README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure cd lake_thermal_structure On Windows 11, open PowerShell in the download directory. Paste and run the entire function definition below before running the two Join-FileParts commands. Each command reports the part being joined and the completed ZIP path. Joining several gigabytes may take a few minutes. function Join-FileParts($Pattern, $OutputFile, [int]$ExpectedParts) { $directory = (Get-Location).ProviderPath $parts = @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $directory -Filter $Pattern -File | Sort-Object Name) if ($parts.Count -ne $ExpectedParts) { throw "Expected $ExpectedParts parts in $directory; found $($parts.Count)." } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $ExpectedParts; $i++) { $expected = $OutputFile + ('.part{0:D3}' -f $i) if ($parts[$i].Name -ne $expected) { throw "Missing or incorrectly named part: $expected" } } $outputPath = Join-Path $directory $OutputFile $temporaryPath = $outputPath + '.joining' $outputStream = [System.IO.File]::Create($temporaryPath) try { foreach ($part in $parts) { Write-Host "Joining $($part.Name)..." $partStream = [System.IO.File]::OpenRead($part.FullName) try { $partStream.CopyTo($outputStream) } finally { $partStream.Dispose() } } } finally { $outputStream.Dispose() } $expectedSize = ($parts | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum if ((Get-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath).Length -ne $expectedSize) { throw "Joined file size does not match the total part size." } Move-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath -Destination $outputPath -Force Write-Host "Completed: $outputPath" } Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip" 8 Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip" 12 New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force lake_thermal_structure | Out-Null Copy-Item README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure Set-Location lake_thermal_structure The commands use built-in macOS and Windows 11 tools. If the optional results ZIP was not downloaded, omit its tar -xf command. Extracting the archives into the same destination reconstructs this layout: lake_thermal_structure/ ├── README.md ├── requirements.txt ├── script/ ├── data/ └── results/ 2.2 Hardware A standard desktop or laptop computer can run the scripts, but the full data workflow is memory intensive. We recommend: RAM: at least 64 GB for the full datasets included here. Storage: at least 25 GB for the extracted repository and generated outputs. Allow at least 65 GB of free space while joining and extracting all downloaded archive parts; the downloaded parts and reconstructed ZIP files can be deleted after successful extraction. GPU: not required. Non-standard hardware: not required. The lightweight Poyang Lake demo dataset requires substantially less memory than the full figure workflows. 2.3 Software Setup and First Run The scripts were developed and tested with Python 3.13.5 on Windows 11. Required Python packages are listed in requirements.txt. Install them and run the lightweight demo from the reconstructed repository root: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python script/demo.py The demo writes its outputs to results/demo/. Full manuscript figures can be regenerated with the commands in Section 6. Generating each figure takes approximately 10 minutes. Figure 4 may take longer time for its large amount of data input. The generated figures were further edited in Adobe Illustrator for publication. This repository contains the species occurrence datasets and environmental raster variables used in the manuscript 'The importance of soil pH maps for the accuracy of plant distribution models'. The study evaluates the impact of incorporating different spatial soil pH datasets (LUCAS vs. SoilGrids) on the accuracy of plant species distribution models (SDMs) across continental (Europe) and regional (the Czech Republic, Austria) scales.

This dataset contains the blended TROPOMI+GOSAT methane observations for May 2024 used in the manuscript entitled Efficient computation of global high-resolution Jacobian matrices for analytical inversions of satellite observations of greenhouse gases: Application to the Integrated Methane Inversion (IMI) version 2.3. This dataset is a frozen subset of the blended TROPOMI+GOSAT methane data product described by Balasus et al. (2023). The data were obtained from the Registry of Open Data on AWS. The original dataset at https://registry.opendata.aws/blended-tropomi-gosat-methane/ is continuously updated. This archive preserves the specific observations used in the manuscript. Reference: Balasus, N., Jacob, D. J., Lorente, A., Maasakkers, J. D., Parker, R. J., Boesch, H., Chen, Z., Kelp, M. M., Nesser, H., and Varon, D. J.: A blended TROPOMI+GOSAT satellite data product for atmospheric methane using machine learning to correct retrieval biases, Atmos. Meas. Tech., 16, 3787–3807, 2023.

Empirically-derived relationships are mainly used to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) in water balance models. Due to a lack of effective factors and correct conceptual relationships, the resulting ET may be inaccurate. Therefore, a hydrological model was developed by combining water balance and bulk transfer theory, called semi-distributed coupled water balance and bulk transfer (SD-CWBT). According to it, a dynamic interrelationship between ET and soil moisture was correctly established to estimate ET via physical concepts. Global gridded ET retrievals, which provide the spatiotemporal distribution of ET at a global scale, including ECMWF Reanalysis v5-Land (ERA5-Land), TERRA, Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and Operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop), were employed to evaluate the model. The results indicated the SD-CWBT, with Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of [0.6, 0.95], [0.68, 0.96], and [12.61, 0.99] for the streamflow and groundwater level simulation, respectively, had better performance compared to the alternatives. Furthermore, the estimated spatiotemporal distributions of ET agreed well with the climatic-vegetation conditions.

Data availability statement This study uses six types of third-party data for flood extent forecasting in Poyang Lake. The SAR-derived surface-water maps are available at https://lake.geodata.cn/data/datadetails.html?dataguid=118284467501001&docid=5 and are described by Li et al. (2025), doi:10.18307/2025.0247. The Copernicus GLO-30 DEM is available at https://doi.org/10.5069/G9028PQB and was provided by the European Space Agency (2024). The GLC_FCS30D land-cover dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8239305 and is described by Zhang et al. (2024), doi:10.5194/essd-16-1353-2024. The CHM_PRE V2 precipitation dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.11888/Atmos.tpdc.300523 and is described by Hu et al. (2025), doi:10.5194/essd-17-3987-2025. The CMFD v2.0 air temperature data are available at https://doi.org/10.11888/Atmos.tpdc.302088, with the original CMFD dataset described by He et al. (2020), doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0369-y. The GLASS MODIS-based surface net radiation product, version V50, is available at https://glass.hku.hk/archive/RN/MODIS/ and is described by Liang et al. (2023), doi:10.11834/jrs.20232462. All the above datasets are freely accessible for academic research through their original repositories or data providers. The data used for model training and evaluation were processed from these third-party datasets following the procedures described in Section 2.

description: This release supports the study “Concurrent burned-area detections are associated with persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon”. Version 1.1.0 adds Supplementary_Data_1_Active_Fire_Analysis.zip, containing the complementary historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS analysis, the fixed protocol, input data, derived matching results, scripts, environment requirements, provenance, checksums, tests and independent verification results. Download and extract this ZIP without changing its folder structure, then open 08_VALIDACION_FUEGO_ACTIVO/START_HERE_REVIEWERS.md. The ZIP is 17,955,692 bytes and contains 59 files. The original cohort archive fire_loss_conversion_peruvian_amazon_v1.0.0.zip and its separate companion files are preserved unchanged. Those historical companions retain the original title, DOI, version and figure numbering. For this release, read START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md and use CITATION_VERSION_1_1_0.cff. The original release remains available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21881539. The study uses a retrospective spatial cohort sampled on a systematic 0.01° lattice in stable forests of the Peruvian Amazon. Hansen Global Forest Change defines first loss during 2014–2021; MapBiomas Peru Collection 3 defines baseline and subsequent land cover; MapBiomas Fire and GABAM define concurrent burned-area detection categories. Persistent conversion requires anthropogenic cover in each of three consecutive post-loss years. The original archive reproduces analyses from derived panels, not the raster-to-panel extraction. The estimates are associational. Thermal observations corroborate nearby combustion but do not validate individual 30 m burned pixels or subsequent land use. No field photographs or field campaign data are included. This dataset release does not publish the manuscript or confidential review correspondence. Author-owned material is covered by the record-level CC BY 4.0 licence. Software in the preserved original code folder retains its included additional MIT licence. NASA data and other third-party materials retain their original terms, attribution and disclaimers and are not relicensed by this deposit. See START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md for details. Funding: This research received no external funding.

We present the dataset (in .csv) of sea surface temperature (SST, in °C), sea surface salinity (SSS), chlorophyll-a (Chl-a, in mg m³) and sea surface CO2 fugacity (fCO2, in µatm) used for the development of the fCO2 model. Recalculated measurements of fCO2 were extracted from cruises with quality control flags A and B in the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas version 2025 (SOCAT v2025, https://doi.org/10.25921/648f-fv35). SST and SSS data were extracted from the L4 product Multi Observation Global Ocean ARMOR3D (https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00052) matching the in situ fCO2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 0.25°. Satellite-derived Chl-a data was extracted from daily images from the ESA Ocean Color Climate Change Initiative 6.0 database (https://www.oceancolour.org/) matching the in situ fCO2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 1 km. We also present the recalculated spatial fields (in .nc) of SST (in °C), SSS, Chl-a (in mg m³), fCO2 (in µatm) and calculated uncertainty (in µatm) for March, April and May between 2010 and 2025, with a spatial resolution of 0.125°.

description: La Malinche Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization (LMCHSR) is a public geospatial dataset of forest canopy height and structural regionalization for an area of interest encompassing the La Montaña Malinche o Matlalcuéyatl Federal Protected Natural Area, Mexico, and the adjacent peripheral area included in the analysis. The 2019 canopy-height raster was produced by integrating three Random Forest models corresponding to Sentinel-2 Level-2A acquisitions on 22 January, 28 March, and 12 April 2019. Each model used the red (B4), red-edge (B5), and shortwave-infrared (B12) bands, together with elevation and slope, as predictors. Canopy heights from CHMv2 (Brandt et al., 2026) served as the response reference after spatial harmonization to the 10 m modeling grid. The date-specific predictions were integrated into a multitemporal canopy-height surface. Structural products were derived from this RF surface on a 20 m analytical grid. They include structural objects, aggregated regions, five canopy-height classes (S01–S05), and connected class patches. An independent set of 20 m structural products was derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map of Lang et al. (2023), with separately determined objects, regions, and five classes (E01–E05). The harmonized source ETH canopy-height raster is not redistributed. The release contains 18 geospatial assets: one area-of-interest boundary, the 2019 RF canopy-height raster (RF 2019), eight RF-derived structural products, and eight ETH2020-derived structural products. Raster and vector files are supplied as GeoTIFF and GeoPackage files, respectively, using the WGS 84 / UTM zone 14N coordinate reference system (CRS; EPSG:32614). The release also includes metadata, dictionaries, a class legend, and Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksums. The two structural classifications were generated independently; matching class codes do not imply identical class definitions or direct temporal forest change.
keywords: Forest canopy height; Canopy-height-based structural regionalization; La Malinche; Mexico; Sentinel-2; Random Forest; CHMv2; Global Canopy Height Map for 2020; Canopy-height-based structural classes

description: De-identified data, analysis code and analysis outputs for a study of ecological restoration ("greening"), wildfire and fire-prevention duties in the Reshuihe watershed (174.7 km²), Xide County, Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, China. Survey. 815 questionnaires submitted online (Tencent Questionnaire) between 26 April and 3 May 2026, with the link forwarded by local government staff, who asked that their office and channels not be named; respondents answered on their own phones and staff had no access to the answers. Convenience sample; 84 submissions came from IP addresses in Liangshan Prefecture, 17 from elsewhere in Sichuan and 714 from outside Sichuan (released as a three-level variable). 73 coded variables, including five three-item Likert constructs (hazard concern, fire-duty burden, project participation, project dependence, perceived welfare) and four post hoc data-quality flags. Bilingual codebook and questionnaire text included. Code and outputs. Structural equation models with robustness checks, measurement-invariance and equivalence tests, and heterogeneity by IP location (R, lavaan); a Google Earth Engine pipeline for Landsat-only NDVI 2000–2025, a 200-basin donor pool, MODIS MCD64A1 burned area, FIRMS active fire, GLC_FCS30D land cover and CHIRPS/ERA5-Land climate; Python scripts for pixel-wise trends with FDR control, synthetic control / synthetic difference-in-differences with placebo inference, and fire activity relative to donor basins. Remote-sensing results. Growing-season NDVI rose across the watershed (median Sen's slope +0.0058 per year, 2000–2025), but no more than in 104 comparable basins: synthetic difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of the 2008 works −0.028 (95% CI −0.068 to 0.012, placebo p = 0.17). Version 2 corrects the description of how the survey data were collected, releases all 815 responses with collection date, completion time and IP-location group, replaces the version 1 remote-sensing files with the exports and outputs of a new Landsat-only pipeline, and corrects two specification issues of the version 1 SEM analysis. See CHANGELOG.md.
keywords: remote sensing; NDVI; environmental governance; ethnic minority; China; ecological restoration; wildfire; fire prevention; Liangshan; Yi; online survey; structural equation modelling; measurement invariance; synthetic control; Landsat NDVI; MODIS MCD64A1; FIRMS

description: Crown length (CL) describes the vertical extent of an individual tree's live crown. Canopy depth (CD) describes the vertical extent of the canopy within a forest stand. Both inform fire behaviour, vegetation and habitat models, yet their global distributions remain poorly resolved. We present global maps of mean CL and CD at 1 km resolution for 2020. We first retrieved CL for individual trees segmented from lidar point clouds, as tree height minus crown-base height. Within each of 1147 reference records on six continents, mean CL was the average of the tree values and CD was the 95th-percentile tree height minus the lowest crown base. Both were related to satellite and environmental predictors using random forest models. Tree-level CL agreed with field measurements and manual annotations with R² = 0.62 and RMSE = 2.63 m. Across 46 validation plots, RMSE was 1.90 m for mean CL and 2.09 m for CD. In the 30 % hold-out set, the mapping models achieved R² = 0.64 for CL and 0.72 for CD, with RMSE of 2.15 m and 2.98 m. Global mean CL and CD were 7.0 m and 14.2 m. Long crowns and deep canopies occurred in equatorial rain forests and humid temperate forests. Savannas, Mediterranean woodlands and dry forests had the smallest values. These maps give the first globally consistent view of the crown layer beneath the canopy top. They can constrain crown geometry in vegetation models, canopy fuel depth in fire models and vertical habitat structure in biodiversity studies.

Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance" (Yiran Li), revision 1 (R1) of the manuscript under review at the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies. This version supersedes version 1, which accompanied the original submission. The package contains the analysis code, the derived data tables and the figures underlying the paper, which presents a global source–receptor accounting of cross-border delta sediment starvation. Local sediment production is routed along the HydroBASINS river network; each dam's trapping is computed from its Brune efficiency and regulated-flow share; large natural lakes retain sediment with and without dams; natural loads are anchored to observed pre-dam values (39 rivers) or to the pristine loads of the Nienhuis et al. (2020) delta inventory; and each delta's dam-induced deficit is split into a domestic and a cross-border part and attributed to the upstream countries responsible. Key results (R1): dams withhold about 5,100 Mt yr⁻¹ of sediment from the world's inventoried deltas, of which about 1,130 Mt yr⁻¹ (22.1%) is withheld by dams in another country; 46 countries are net downstream bearers (25 of them bearing at least 1 Mt yr⁻¹); about 156 million people live on national delta parts that have lost at least a tenth of their sediment supply, mostly to foreign dams, 87% of them in Bangladesh and Egypt. Leading upstream sources: India, the United States, China, Ethiopia and Brazil. Contents: the analysis scripts (sediment_routing.py and the revision scripts run by run_all_r1.sh), the builders of the manuscript, Supplementary Material and response letter (build_all.sh), all derived CSV and JSON tables, Figures 1–5 and the graphical abstract. README_R1.md documents the input data, the run order, the method and all changes from version 1. A clean-room run from the public raw inputs (HydroBASINS, BasinATLAS, Global Dam Watch, the GlobalDeltaData of Nienhuis et al., the delta extents of Edmonds et al., the WorldPop 2020 grid, Natural Earth and World Bank GDP) reproduces every derived table byte for byte. The reviewer reports are confidential and are not included. No generative-AI tools were used to produce any figure or graphical artwork; all figures are data plots generated by the included code.

Dataset Information Current Version: v2 (changelog at end of repository Contacts: Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk) and Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) The Surface Ocean CO2 Mapping program entered its second phase (SOCOMv2) with a range of experiments which provides a coordinated, community-driven framework to evaluate surface ocean fugacity of CO2 in seawater (sfCO2) reconstructions and derived air–sea CO2 fluxes under present-day observational constraints. This repository holds the dataset used within a Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model (GOBM) subsampling experiment designated Experiment 2, where nine fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) reconstruction methodologies reconstructed five GOBMs from the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (and one from 2024). The analysis and results of the study are presented in Roobaert et al. (in prep). How to reference? If you use these data for a new analysis or publication, we request that you contact Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) and Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk). This will allow the authors, and the SOCOM community the opportunity to contribute and be considered for co-authorship, depending on their level of involvement. If these data are used please reference the orginial study (Roobaert et al. 2026) and the repository with the version. Data format This dataset includes five individual zip files which contain a single netCDF file. Within each netCDF, the model fCO2sw and air-sea CO2 fluxes alongside the sfCO2 reconstructions and resulting air-sea CO2 fluxes. Ancillary information including for example model sea surface tmeperature and salinity, gas transfer, wind speed and a consistent mask where all data products provide an fCO2 estimate, are included within each file to aid interpretation of the data. Each zip file contains a netCDF file with the corresponding naming: SOCOMv2_Ex2_<model_name>_full_variables_<version>.nc where <model_name> is the model name from the five models, and <version> represents the dataset version. Model naming is shown in the table below: Model Name CESM_ETHZ_r1 FESOM2_REcoM IPSL_r1 MRI_ESM2_2 NorESM_vGCB2024 We refer the user to the netCDF file for the full set of avaiable variables but as a quick start: Model fCO2 are found under: model_sfco2 Model air-sea CO2 fluxes are found under: model_flux The corresponding data product fCO2 and air-sea CO2 fluxes are found by replacing 'model' with the corresponding dataproduct name. For example: VLIZ-SOMFFN_sfco2 Avaiable data products are: Dataproduct Name CarboScope-v2 CMEMS-LSCE-FFNN CSIR-ML6 JMA-MLR NIES-ML3 OceanSODA-ETHZv2 pCO2Residual UExP-FNN-U-v2 VLIZ-SOMFFN Changelog Version Changes since previous version v2 Updated CarboScope to a new version (now named CarboScope-v2) v1 Initial release of the dataset ready for submission of the supporting manuscript. A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes This dataset maps potential habitat within populated, human-used landscapes on a ~1 km² hexagonal discrete global grid (ISEA3H, resolution 16; 1.18491 km² cells). Spatial domain: all files cover the 114,791,301 land cells whose centroid lies at or north of 60°S. Antarctica and other land south of 60°S are not included. For each cell, the dataset provides: the cell centroid; country (FAO GAUL 2024, with de facto assignment for disputed areas); counts of 10 m land-cover pixels: Dynamic World 2024, ESA WorldCover 2021, Global Pasture Watch and the Spatial Database of Planted Trees v2.0; land area, habitat area and habitat fraction of land; population: WorldPop R2025A, 2024, 100 m; classification into 'Populated' and 'Shared' Landscapes. 'Populated Landscapes' are cells where more than 1% of land is non-habitat (crop, built-up, pasture or tree crops) and population density is at least 1 person per km² of land. 'Shared Landscapes' are Populated Landscapes in which at least 20% of land is habitat. Globally: Populated Landscapes cover 26.14 million km² (20.5% of land); Shared Landscapes cover 18.87 million km² (14.8% of land; 72.2% of Populated Landscapes); 37.75% of the population lives in Shared Landscapes. Files dgg_isea3h16_land_shapefiles.zip: the land grid as 377 zipped shapefiles (10° tiles). Cells touch Natural Earth 10m or OpenStreetMap land, with a 200 m buffer. dgg_cells_shared_landscapes_dataset.csv.gz: per-cell results: centroid, country assignment, pixel counts, population, land and habitat areas and fractions, and landscape classes (gzip CSV, 33 columns). dataset_summaries.zip: global_summary.csv and country_summary.csv, with areas, fractions and the fraction of population in Shared Landscapes. DATA_DICTIONARY.md: definitions of every column and file format. Code: https://github.com/njdepsky/SharedLandscapes (MIT). The grid script accepts any bounding box, for example a global grid. Article: Ellis et al., Data in Brief (2026). Licence and attribution: Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0. The grid is derived from OpenStreetMap data, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Dynamic World: "This dataset is produced for the Dynamic World Project by Google in partnership with National Geographic Society and the World Resources Institute." The inputs (Dynamic World, ESA WorldCover, Global Pasture Watch, SDPT v2.0, FAO GAUL 2024, WorldPop, Natural Earth) are used under their respective licences.

description: Processed datasets underlying all figures and tables of the manuscript "Quantifying the Global Impact of Forcing Variability on Hydrological and Land Surface Model Performance: A Multi-Model Evaluation". The data cover four global hydrological and land-surface models (HTESSEL, JULES, mHM, PCR-GLOBWB) driven by four precipitation forcings (EM-Earth, ERA5-Land, MSWEP, W5E5) over 1981–2019 at 0.1° resolution: precipitation differences and water-balance closure, anomaly correlation of TWSa, evapotranspiration and runoff against GravIS, FLUXCOM and GRUN, streamflow KGE at 1445 GRDC gauges, precipitation elasticity of runoff and evapotranspiration, and long-term mean discharge for the forcing-versus-model variance decomposition. Each zip contains one analysis folder; README.md and the README_*.md files describe all variables. The code that reads these files is archived separately (see related works).

description: This dataset contains processed fire perimeter records from four wildfire datasets: the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CalFire; 1990–2025), Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS; 1990–2024), the Global Fire Atlas (Atlas; 2001–2025), and the FIREDpy-based country-level dataset (FIRED; 2000–2024). Atlas and FIRED are derived from MODIS imagery. CalFire records are limited to fire events larger than 1 km². All four shapefiles include fire identifiers, ignition date, year and decade, burned area (size_km2), Northern/Southern California flags, and WUI classification attributes from intersecting fire perimeters with WUI boundaries (FireType: WUI vs Wildland; reachWUI; reachUrban). CalFire further includes containment date, ignition cause, climate and terrain variables (temperature, vapor pressure deficit, precipitation, wind, elevation, slope, NDVI, and land cover), ignition-based WUI classes derived by matching Global Fire Atlas ignition points to CalFire perimeters (IgnWUI; IgnType: WUIIgnite, WUISpread, or Wildland), the within-perimeter WUI burned-area fraction (WUIfrac), 4-day mean Canadian Fire Weather Index moisture codes (FFMC_4d, DMC_4d, DC_4d), Santa Ana wind occurrence flags for Southern California fires (SAW), and within-perimeter land-cover fractions from MCD12Q1 FAO-LCCS1 2020 (fracFor, fracGrass, fracShrub, fracSG). A full field list is provided in CalFire_added_fields.txt. The four perimeter datasets are provided as compressed Shapefiles. These data are intended to support research on fire size distribution, fire behavior, land-fire interactions, and WUI risk assessment.

R code, unit tests, saved summary tables and figure-source tables for a spatial analysis of 197 Palaeolithic findspots (59 source references) in Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India (Wainganga-Wardha basin). The primary analysis estimates how site intensity varies with distance to drainage of increasing river size (WRIS stream order >= k, k = 3 to 9), using a down-weighted Poisson point-process likelihood with a ridge prior, spatial cluster-bootstrap inference, spatial cross-validation, a lineament-distance negative control and a robustness matrix. The analysis design was frozen and checksummed before the site-water models were fitted; the manifest is included. The primary hypothesis (intensity falls with distance to larger rivers) was not supported; the association depends on site classification, and exploratory analyses are labelled as such. Contents: scripts S01-S19, tests, saved result tables, figure-source tables, PDF figures, renv lockfile (R 4.5.2). Not included: exact site coordinates, the 1 km coarsened site table, and raw third-party data layers (WRIS, HydroRIVERS, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap, Global Dam Watch), which must be obtained from their providers. Limitations: modern water bodies are a proxy for Pleistocene water; legacy survey bias; mixed coordinate quality; undated typology; no field validation.
keywords: palaeolithic; nagpur; chandrapur; central india; archaeological survey; river size; spatial point process

description: This archive contains the R code, dataset provenance, input-file fingerprints, summary data, validation outputs and reference figures supporting the study “Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification”. The analysis covers 2000–2020 at a 0.05-degree working grid and distinguishes five temporally stable vegetation classes. Ecosystem-stratified generalised additive models include site random intercepts and AR(1) errors. The primary model includes a spherical spatial smooth and CO2; a matched 2 × 2 design tests sensitivity to these two terms. Trend inference uses Newey–West standard errors and global Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Global and ecosystem summaries use actual pixel area, with spatial-block bootstrap intervals and spatial-block cross-validation. The archive includes pooled out-of-fold level, trend and sign diagnostics, area-representative held-out trend shares, five CO2 spatial-support scenarios, and machine-readable CSV versions of all 30 parts of Supplementary Tables 1–9. The environment–CO2 baseline and unexplained-residual shares are descriptive co-directional trend components. Their association with composite human pressure is exploratory and does not identify causal effects of human activity. Raw third-party datasets, high-resolution derived rasters, site-level source and prediction tables, and model objects are excluded where redistribution rights are unclear. Users must acquire source data from the official providers and follow the documented reconstruction workflow. The included Natural Earth coastline is public domain.
keywords: solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence; vegetation trends; ecosystem type; global change; environmental baseline; residual trend; generalised additive model; spatial-block cross-validation; area weighting; Newey–West HAC; false discovery rate; reproducible research

description: AZ-Hydro: Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use, 1896–2099 (v1.2) A 2 km-resolution gridded dataset of Arizona groundwater and surface-water withdrawals, irrigation consumptive use, and pumping-induced stream capture, spanning 204 years (1896–2099), with per-pixel uncertainty from a six-component framework and a well-level package for ~170,000 registered consumptive wells. Companion data archive for Majumdar et al. (submitted to Nature Scientific Data; preprint https://doi.org/10.31223/X56N63) and Majumdar et al. (in prep., AGU Earth’s Future). Version 1.2 (code release v1.2.0). See What’s new in v1.2 below. What’s in this deposit File Size Contents Audience az-hydro-headline.7z ~8.7 GB Self-contained subset of every key output: six-band augmented per-pixel, per-year withdrawal, consumptive-use, and stream capture rasters (prediction, σ, CV, SNR, lower and upper 95 % CI); the GeoParquet well package; per-basin and per-sub-basin time series; the CAP shortage-scenario sweep; era-mean and trend figures; validation and intercomparison outputs. Most users want this. Reviewers and downstream users of the published product az-hydro-data.7z ~80 GB Full reproducibility archive (~220 GB uncompressed): everything in the headline archive plus the raw inputs, cross-validation outputs, intermediate input stacks, and per-component uncertainty rasters (σ_MACA, σ_model, σ_irr, σ_LULC, σ_GW, σ_USBR, σ_CU). Anyone re-running the pipeline from scratch az-hydro-1.2.0.zip ~64 MB Tagged source-code release (Python pipeline, GEE export and upload scripts, documentation), identical to the GitHub repository at tag v1.2.0. Anyone running the pipeline README.md, HEADLINE_README.md, ADWR_readme.txt ~50 KB Current copies of the guides inside the archives: Data/README.md (full archive), Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive), and the ADWR folder’s readme.txt. They supersede the copies inside the .7z files, which predate the final author list and citations. Everyone Inside each .7z, Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive) or Data/README.md (full archive) gives the per-directory inventory and the external-source citations. The standalone copies of these files in this deposit are the current versions. How to unpack the .7z files The archives use LZMA2 with solid-block compression, which macOS Archive Utility cannot open. Use one of: macOS: Keka or The Unarchiver Windows: 7-Zip, WinRAR, or Bandizip Linux: p7zip (for example apt install p7zip-full, then 7z x az-hydro-data.7z) What’s new in v1.2 Post-2026 Colorado River shortage. The central projection now uses the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines (U.S. Department of the Interior, August 2026), which reduce Arizona’s Colorado River apportionment by 760 kAF yr⁻¹ (CAP delivery factor 0.49, groundwater boost 7.5). The guidelines cover 2027–2028; 2029–2099 hold that latest official condition as a stand-in for continued shortage, not as a forecast. v1.0–v1.1 held the Tier 1 cut (512 kAF yr⁻¹) through 2099. Projected 2027–2099 groundwater withdrawal is 5.5 % higher and surface-water withdrawal 5.5 % lower than in v1.1; total withdrawal and all 1896–2026 predictions are unchanged. CAP scenario sweep. A ninth scenario applies the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines: 652 kAF yr⁻¹ of CAP delivery, the 900 kAF yr⁻¹ post-Tier baseline less the 248 kAF yr⁻¹ by which the guidelines’ 760 kAF yr⁻¹ Arizona reduction exceeds the Tier 1 cut that baseline is taken to include. It adds 1.30 MAF of groundwater pumping over 2027–2060 and 3.15 MAF over 2027–2099. The other scenarios are unchanged. Uncertainty ensemble. The ensemble members now apply the same dynamic CAP caps and floors as the central partition (a missing import had disabled them). σ for the groundwater and surface-water categories changes in every year; σ for total withdrawal does not. The scenario sweep keeps its full-delivery counterfactual. ADWR partner CSVs (Outputs/.../ADWR/). In v1.1, 14 of the 16 CSVs listed every basin-year twice, because the export also picked up the all-basin aggregate files. Each row now appears once, and Total_Predicted is built from the same per-basin series as the other categories, so Total_GW + Total_SW = Total_Predicted holds row by row. Basin totals count boundary pixels in every basin they touch, so summing basins exceeds the statewide total by about 2–3 %; statewide totals are in Annual_Summaries/. Headline archive now also includes the out-of-distribution probability rasters (OOD_Rasters/, 68 MB). GEE assets for the AZ-Hydro Explorer moved to projects/azhydro/assets/az-wu-v1-2/. Methods overview AZ-Hydro is a physics-constrained machine learning pipeline: XGBRF prediction of total annual withdrawal depth per 2 km pixel, trained on ADWR metered pumping records (1984–2024) with 22 predictors (actual and reference ET, precipitation, effective precipitation, temperature, land-cover fractions and densities, irrigated and groundwater-irrigation fractions, soil properties, water-table depth, well, surface-water-rights and canal densities, watershed streamflow, and pixel coordinates). Climate, ET, and land-cover inputs from different eras are joined into continuous 1896–2099 series by overlap-period bias correction. Density-ratio partition of the total into irrigation and non-irrigation withdrawals from groundwater and surface water, with consumptive use derived as CU = irrigation efficiency × irrigation withdrawal. The few free partition parameters were tuned to statewide USGS and ADWR records (USGS OFR 94-476, 1915–1990; USGS Circulars, 1950–2015; ADWR Annual Report totals and the 2019 ADWR shares); the machine learning totals are never adjusted. Six-component uncertainty quantification: σ_MACA (5 GCMs), σ_model (10 XGBRF seeds), σ_irr (irrigated-area input), σ_LULC (4 USGS land-use scenarios), σ_GW (5 recent well-registry snapshots), and σ_USBR (5 Upper Colorado River streamflow members), combined in quadrature and propagated to consumptive use (σ_CU). Stream capture index combining connectivity (exponential decay with water-table depth) and nearby surface-water availability, with pumping and connectivity uncertainty propagated to the capture volumes. Key validations Statewide agency reconciliation (calibration adequacy, not an independent test): 2017 ADWR total withdrawal 6.81 vs 7.00 MAF (−2.7 %); 2015 USGS groundwater withdrawal 2.96 vs 3.09 MAF (−4.1 %); 2019 ADWR irrigation share 74.2 % vs 72 %; 1955 and 1980 pumping peaks under-predicted by 6–11 %, with every reported total inside the model’s 95 % σ_total interval. Independent comparisons against USGS NHM withdrawals and consumptive use, USGS Reitz irrigation rasters, the USGS public-supply reanalysis, and CAP and SRP delivery records (statewide surface water within 0.8 % of the 1985–2024 CAP + SRP mean). WestWater Research (2026) CAP shortage anchor: Basic Coordination cumulative additional groundwater pumping 7.24 MAF over 2027–2060 vs 8.0 MAF (−9.5 %); Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF vs 8.7 MAF (the gap reflects AZ-Hydro’s no-regulatory-ceiling framing). CAP delivery shortage scenario sweep Nine scenarios (the no-cut Baseline_900kAF; DCP Tiers 0, 1, 2a, 2b, and 3; the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines; WestWater Basic Coordination; Extreme Shortage) re-partitioned over 2026–2099. Cumulative additional groundwater pumping over 2027–2060: Operating Guidelines 1.30 MAF, DCP Tier 1 4.05 MAF, DCP Tier 3 10.69 MAF, Basic Coordination 7.24 MAF, Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF. Basin and per-pixel maps, cumulative σ, and signal-to-noise figures are included for the 2027–2060 and 2027–2099 windows. External datasets required to reproduce the pipeline (not redistributed here) The pipeline reads four USGS ScienceBase data products that must be downloaded separately: USGS NHM withdrawals (Haynes et al. 2023): irrigation withdrawals and efficiency by HUC12, 2000–2020 USGS NHM consumptive use reanalysis (Martin et al. 2023; Martin et al. 2025): irrigation consumptive use by HUC12 USGS public-supply reanalysis (Luukkonen et al. 2023; Alzraiee et al. 2024): public-supply withdrawals by HUC12 USGS Reitz historical ET (Reitz et al. 2023; Reitz, Sanford & Saxe 2023): 800 m gridded ET Bundled here directly: ADWR Well Registry and metered pumping records, GW basin / AMA-INA / CAP / SRP / streamflow / USBR vectors, HarDWR water rights (Lisk et al. 2024), GRAIN canal network (Suresh et al. 2026), and the Ma et al. (2026) water-table depth. See Data/README.md inside each .7z for the exact file names and folders. description: This dataset provides gridded forest canopy structure inputs developed for the lidar-based initialization of the Ecosystem Demography model (ED v3.0), as described in Ma et al. (2023). It includes mean canopy height and canopy height histograms derived from NASA GEDI and ICESat-2 observations, together with tree canopy cover from the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS), at a spatial resolution of 0.01°. These products characterize spatial variation in canopy height and the distribution of observed canopy heights within each grid cell. They were developed to connect satellite observations of forest structure with mechanistic ecosystem modeling and can support initialization and evaluation of other forest and vegetation models. Data contents The repository contains five GeoTIFF files: Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, calculated from filtered GEDI L2A version 002 RH100 observations. Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_hist_count.tif: GEDI canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, derived from filtered ICESat-2 ATL08 version 005 observations. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_hist_count.tif: ICESat-2 canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. CGLS_forest_percent_2019_001deg.tif: Tree canopy cover percentage for 2019, aggregated from the native 100 m CGLS product to 0.01°. Source observations and processing The study used GEDI observations acquired from March 2019 through August 2021 and ICESat-2 observations acquired from October 2018 through October 2021. GEDI observations cover approximately 51°S–51°N, while ICESat-2 provides observations beyond this latitude range. Observations were quality filtered and assigned to 0.01° grid cells. The filtering criteria documented in the paper were: GEDI: quality_flag = 1, sensitivity > 0.95, and RH100 > 5 m. ICESat-2: dem_removal_flag = 0, canopy_flag = 1, cloud_flag_atm < 4, and h_canopy > 5 m. Canopy height histograms contain 90 bins spanning 5–50 m at 0.5 m intervals. Each histogram layer records sample counts rather than normalized probabilities. Mean canopy height summarizes the retained observations within each grid cell. The products pool observations across the acquisition periods and do not represent annual time series. Use in model initialization In the associated study, canopy height histograms were used to index height-based lookup tables generated by ED v3.0. Model states associated with each height bin were weighted by the observed sample counts, preserving variation in canopy height within a grid cell. Tree canopy cover was then used to scale forest estimates to the whole grid cell. The histograms describe the distribution of sampled canopy heights across footprints or segments within a grid cell; they are not vertical foliage profiles or distributions of individual tree heights. Spatial coverage and sampling density vary because both lidar missions collect observations along orbital tracks. Cells without retained observations should not be interpreted as having zero canopy height. Associated publication Ma, L., et al. (2023). Spatial heterogeneity of global forest aboveground carbon stocks and fluxes constrained by spaceborne lidar data and mechanistic modeling. Global Change Biology, 29, 3378–3394. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16682 Please cite this dataset and the associated publication when using these products.

description: This repository contains datasets, R scripts and spatial products for assessing particulate organic carbon (POC) and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) in global grassland topsoils (0–30 cm). Grassland_Scenario_A.csv: Grassland SOC, POC and MAOC observations, geographic coordinates and environmental predictors for Scenario A, combining CHELSA climate and HWSD soil data. Grassland_Scenario_B.csv: The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario B, combining CHELSA climate and SoilGrids soil data. Grassland_Scenario_C.csv: The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario C, combining WorldClim climate and HWSD soil data. Grassland_Scenario_D.csv: The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario D, combining WorldClim climate and SoilGrids soil data. run_POC_A_QRF.r: R script for training, evaluating and applying the Scenario A quantile regression forest model to predict grassland POC concentrations. It includes repeated five-fold cross-validation, variable-importance estimation and spatial prediction. run_MAOC_A_QRF.r: R script for training, evaluating and applying the Scenario A quantile regression forest model to predict grassland MAOC concentrations. It includes repeated five-fold cross-validation, variable-importance estimation and spatial prediction. Grassland V6.R: R script for statistical analyses and figure generation, including observed carbon distributions, prediction maps, model performance, variable importance, partial dependence plots, and carbon stock and density summaries across climate zones, aridity zones and soil groups.

description: This article examines the theoretical and practical aspects of improving the organization of medicine storage, receipt, inventory management, and dispensing processes in community pharmacies. Particular attention is paid to establishing appropriate organizational conditions for maintaining the quality, safety, and effectiveness of pharmaceutical products, managing storage facilities, monitoring temperature and humidity, controlling expiration dates, and maintaining pharmaceutical documentation. The importance of Good Pharmacy Practice (GPP), Good Storage Practice (GSP), and Good Distribution Practice (GDP) principles in modern pharmacy management is also discussed. The study is based on a theoretical analysis of scientific literature, international pharmaceutical guidelines, and organizational management approaches. description: MATLAB code, model inputs, processed results, and figure scripts supporting Dominant Controls on Soil Carbon and Nutrient Dynamics Across Ecosystems: A Global Sensitivity Analysis. The study examines 81 soil biogeochemical parameters across 17 sites using elementary-effects screening and variance-based sensitivity analysis (VBSA). Transient experiments at Chamau examine selected parameter perturbations from three initial conditions. Seven targets are considered: soil organic carbon (SOC), mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC), particulate organic carbon (POC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), soil total nitrogen (STN), soil total phosphorus (STP), and soil total potassium (STK). Unzip all the files to ensure the correct file structure. And a README file is provided for the detailed model setup and analysis workflow.

Analysis scripts and derived data products behind the figures and numerical claims of Dryden & Duncan, "Ocean acidification, compounding anthropogenic stressors and marine water chemistry: evidence, regime-shift risk and implications for marine life". Contents: the winter aragonite threshold classification for all three zonation schemes; the same pipeline restricted to the polar and subpolar zone; the MODIS-Aqua equatorial Atlantic chlorophyll trend test; the figure build scripts; the derived 1-degree winter saturation and trend grids; the PyCO2SYS recomputation of aragonite saturation at the study sites with its per-point uncertainty; and the independent verification block. Primary datasets are not redistributed. OceanSODA-ETHZ v2025, SPOTS, GLODAP, CODAP-NA, World Ocean Atlas 2023 and the MODIS-Aqua ocean-colour products are public, carry their own DOIs, and are listed in README.md with the accessions needed to obtain them. Each script run against the original file reproduces the published values exactly. Expected outputs are tabulated in README.md so that any discrepancy is immediately visible. The polar-zone script deliberately reports the measured present state and no projection; the reason, a coverage artefact caused by seasonal ice in the trend mask, is documented in both the script header and the paper's Methods. Version 7 (October 2026) adds GOES_R1_graded_threshold_package.zip, the material behind the revised manuscript (revision R1 for BMC Marine Science): the graded ecological reference threshold (Omega 3.3 equatorward of 10 degrees to 1.6 poleward of 60 degrees), the winter aragonite saturation grids for 1982 to 2024 with the per-cell trend and the mask, the 1-degree block-mean MODIS-Aqua weights (net primary production, calcite and chlorophyll, 2019 to 2021) used to weight the water below its threshold, the month-by-month version of that weighting, the Monte Carlo, block-bootstrap and structural uncertainty with projections counted from 2023, the sea-surface-temperature variant of the threshold, and the scripts for Figures 1 to 3, S1 and S2 of the revised paper. Every script was re-run from the package before deposit: the numerical scripts reproduce the deposited results to rounding (two of them, run against the raw OceanSODA-ETHZ file, reproduce the deposited grids and JSON exactly), and the figure scripts reproduce the deposited PNG files byte for byte. Primary datasets are not redistributed; the README lists them with their accessions. CC BY 4.0.

description: This repository provides Part 1 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering May 2018 to October 2022. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 1 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 2, covering November 2022 to July 2026, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23585026).

Vessel detections with Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from 2019 to 14 days ago. Multiyear detection of vessels with respective length, speed and orientation estimates based on deep-learning models applied to electro-optical imagery (RGB and near-infrared) at 10-m resolution covering most exclusive economic zones and marine protected areas across the ocean. Sentinel-2 detections are based on electro-optical imagery at 10-m resolution. Compared with our published Sentinel-1 detections based on SAR imagery at 20-m resolution, Sentinel-2 allows detecting smaller vessels with all types of vessel materials, in contrast with the weakness of SAR imagery on revealing vessels made of wood and fiberglass. Sentinel-2 also images the wakes of moving vessels, which further increase the detectability of small vessels and allow us to infer the vessels’ speed and orientation.The rich information contained in the optical imagery can be used to map not only vessel presence, but also vessel activities such as vessel encounters and bottom trawling. Sentinel-2 also covers more area of the ocean than Sentinel-1, and the novel neural-net detection approach does not require the exclusion of near-shore regions (as opposed to the CFAR approach), allowing detection of vessels in highly-packed areas all the way to the shoreline where most human activity is concentrated. Overall, with Sentinel-2 imagery we are able to detect about 3 times more vessels, “see” a broader range of vessel lengths and types, and infer more information of vessel activities than in our previous mapping using Sentinel-1 imagery.

Universität Potsdam, 2026. Verweise auf Abbildungen, Tabellen und Abschnitte beziehen sich auf diesen Bericht. Die Methoden sind dort in Kapitel 3 beschrieben; diese README fasst nur zusammen, was zum Lesen der Dateien nötig ist.
