Produkte (Ordner- und Dateinamen): Kürzel Produkt Zeitraum zeitliche Auflösung Gitterzellen in Brandenburg gimms-lai4g GIMMS LAI4g (Cao et al., 2023a, b) 1982–2020 halbmonatlich (1. und 15. des Monats) 516 hiq-lai HiQ-LAI (Yan et al., 2023, 2024) 2000–2022 8 Tage 1876 si-lai-fpar SI LAI/FPAR (Pu et al., 2023, 2024) 2000–2022 8 Tage 1502 Zeiträume. Für GIMMS LAI4g werden drei Zeiträume ausgewertet: die gesamte Reihe 1982–2020, der rekonstruierte Abschnitt 1982–2003 und der beobachtete Abschnitt 2004–2020. Der Datensatz ist an der Bruchstelle 2004 inkonsistent (Abschnitt 4.1 und 5.1 des Berichts). Trends über die gesamte Reihe 1982–2020 und für den rekonstruierten Abschnitt 1982–2003 sind deshalb nicht belastbar und nur zum Vergleich enthalten. HiQ-LAI und SI LAI/FPAR werden über ihre gesamte Reihe 2000–2022 ausgewertet. Regionen (Ordner- und Dateinamen): brandenburg = gesamtes Untersuchungsgebiet, nord = Nordbrandenburg, sued = Südbrandenburg. Die Grenze ist die Nordkante der Zellreihe, in der Kyritz liegt; jede Zelle wird nach der Lage ihres Mittelpunkts zugeordnet (Abschnitt 3.1, Abbildung 2). Berlin gehört nicht zum Untersuchungsgebiet. Ausgewertet sind nur Zellen, die zu mindestens 75 % in Brandenburg liegen. Landnutzungsklassen. Die Spalten tragen englische Kurznamen: Spalte Klasse im Bericht CLC-Codes (Tabelle 7) pineforest Nadelwald (in Brandenburg überwiegend Kiefer) 312 otherforest sonstiger Wald 141, 311, 313, 324 cropland Acker 211, 222, 242, 243 grassland Grünland 231, 321, 322, 411 other Restklasse (bebaute Flächen, Gewässer, Abbau, Sand u. a.) übrige Codes Die Restklasse wird im Bericht nicht ausgewertet; ihr LAI ist in der Entmischung auf 0–0,1 begrenzt. Einheiten. LAI in m²/m². Sen-Steigungen (sen_slope, *_slope) in m²/m² pro Jahr; der Bericht nennt sie teils zusätzlich pro Dekade (× 10). Phänologische Termine als Tag im Jahr (DOY), deren Trends in Tagen pro Jahr. Winterzeitraum. Werte der Kompositen mit Beginn zwischen 15. November und 25. Januar sind in allen Produkten und Zeiträumen entfernt (Abschnitt 2.6 des Berichts; Ursache: unzuverlässige Winterwerte der LAI-Produkte). Dezember und Januar haben daher keine Monatstrends; der November beruht bei GIMMS LAI4g nur auf seiner ersten Hälfte. Einzige Ausnahme sind die Dateien mit dem Zusatz _ganzjahr (siehe unten). Signifikanz (significance, *_sig): *** p < 0,001, ** p < 0,01, * p < 0,05, ns nicht signifikant, n/a nicht berechnet (zu wenige Werte). 2. zeitreihen/ – entmischter LAI je Landnutzungsklasse Datei Inhalt im Bericht gimms-lai4g/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv GIMMS LAI4g, 1982–2020, halbmonatlich, ohne Winterzeitraum Abb. 3, 5, 9, 12–17; Grundlage aller GIMMS-Trends gimms-lai4g/{brandenburg,nord,sued}_ganzjahr.csv wie oben, aber mit Winterzeitraum Abb. 8 (mittlerer Jahresgang) hiq-lai/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv HiQ-LAI, 2000–2022, 8 Tage, ohne Winterzeitraum Grundlage der HiQ-Trends si-lai-fpar/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv SI LAI/FPAR, 2000–2022, 8 Tage, ohne Winterzeitraum Grundlage der SI-Trends Spalten: datetime (Beginn des Kompositums), dann je Klasse der entmischte LAI (pineforest, grassland, otherforest, cropland, other). Nadelwald = 1,0 bei HiQ-LAI) sind möglich. description: This dataset contains the global crop calendar training and validation data used in the manuscript “Enhancing WorldCereal crop calendars with land surface phenology and machine learning” (Moletto-Lobos et al., 2026). It includes harmonized reference crop calendar points derived from GEOGLAM Crop Monitor, USDA-FAS, JRC ASAP, and FAO sources, together with phenology-based samples retrieved from MODIS Aqua NDVI Land Surface Phenology (LSP) time series and ERA5-Land climate variables. The dataset is organized into two main seasonal groups that follow the nomenclature used in the manuscript: S1 = Winter crops (equivalent to winter cereals in the paper) Includes reference and LSP-derived Start of Season (SOS) and End of Season (EOS) dates, including explicitly modeled dormancy periods. S2 = Summer crops (equivalent to summer cropping systems in the paper) Includes SOS and EOS samples for rainfed and monsoon-driven summer crops, corresponding to the “summer season” definition of the study.

description: Daily ISOP (Improved Synthetic Ocean Profile) synthetic temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific (99°E–170°E, 20°S–66°N) for 1 January–31 December 2015. The product was developed by the authors following the methodology of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (Helber et al., 2013), with minor modifications. As described in the accompanying manuscript (Dan et al.), ISOP employs a three-layer vertical structure model (mixed layer, thermocline layer and deep quiescent layer) and uses a variational method combined with historical profile EOF statistics to project satellite sea surface observations onto the subsurface, generating three-dimensional temperature and salinity fields. Its satellite inputs are OISSTv2.1 daily 1/4° sea surface temperature, AVISO/DUACS global 1/8° multi-satellite merged sea surface height anomaly, and the Copernicus 1/8° sea surface salinity merged product. The product extends to a maximum depth of 1000 m (47 levels) at 1/4° horizontal resolution. Observational validation shows that its temperature and salinity errors are comparable to those of the HYCOM and GLORYS12V1 reanalyses, with grid-point temporal and daily spatial correlation coefficients of steric sea surface height with AVISO SLA of 0.874 and 0.897, respectively. The archive contains 365 daily NetCDF files named YYYYMMDD_isop.nc (20150101–20151231); temperature is in degrees Celsius and salinity in PSU, with missing values masked. Data are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Contact: Bo Dan (danb1991@163.com).
keywords: ocean data assimilation; ISOP; synthetic temperature and salinity profiles; satellite-derived ocean subsurface; Northwestern Pacific; sea surface height

description: Model code and simulation output for a global sensitivity study of earthen berms in dryland valleys. Each run is a 100-year Landlab simulation driven by CLIGEN storms for Tucson, Arizona, run once with a berm and once without it, using the same storms. description: Description This dataset provides estimates of net land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) and their component fluxes from the three bookkeeping models used in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026): BLUE (Hansis et al., 2015), LUCE (Qin et al., 2024), and OSCAR (Gasser et al., 2020). Peat drainage emissions are from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021), and peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). The dataset further includes the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026, including estimates from national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset also includes global and gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL), which is the difference in ELUC between a simulation with transient carbon densities and a simulation with pre-industrial carbon densities. The reported net ELUC estimates already include the environmental contribution (δL). Net ELUC and its component fluxes are available as global and national annual time series for 1850–2025. Net ELUC is also available as gridded annual time series (0.25° resolution) for 1959–2025. The data describe CO2 emissions and removals expressed as mass of carbon (C). For ELUC and its component fluxes, positive values denote emissions and negative values denote removals. The sign convention for δL is explained below. Empty cells in .xlsx files denote missing values. The dataset contains 20 files: One .xlsx file with global estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) Fourteen .xlsx files with country-level estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR, one for each of the net and component fluxes listed below (units: TgC/yr) Two NetCDF files with gridded net ELUC estimates for BLUE and LUCE (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) One .xlsx file with the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One .xlsx file with the global estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One NetCDF file with the gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) Global, country-level, and gridded data The dataset includes the following net and component fluxes. The identifiers shown in monospace are used in the corresponding country-level filenames and as worksheet names in the file with global estimates. “SC” denotes shifting cultivation, and “nonforest” refers to shrub and herbaceous vegetation: net-eluc (net ELUC): Net CO2 emissions from land-use change. clearing-allveg-total (deforestation and clearing of other vegetation (total)): Total CO2 emissions from deforestation and the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent clearing and clearing within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-allveg-total ((re-)growth of forest and other vegetation (total)): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of forests and shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent (re-)growth and (re-)growth within shifting cultivation cycles. wood-harvest-management (wood harvest & other management): CO2 emissions from the decay of harvested wood products and residues left on site, and CO2 removals through regrowth following harvest. cropland-pasture-urban (cropland-pasture-urban transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between cropland, pasture, and urban areas. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): CO2 emissions from peat drainage and anthropogenic peat fires. Peat drainage emissions are the average of estimates from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021). Peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation. clearing-forest-sc (deforestation in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from deforestation within shifting cultivation cycles. clearing-nonforest-permanent (permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 emissions from the permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation. clearing-nonforest-sc (clearing of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-forest-permanent (permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation): CO2 removals through forest growth and regrowth following permanent afforestation and reforestation. regrowth-forest-sc (forest (re-)growth in SC cycles): CO2 removals through forest regrowth within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-nonforest-permanent (permanent (re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation following permanent land-use changes. regrowth-nonforest-sc ((re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 removals through the regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. Components 2–6 sum to net ELUC (component 1). Components 7–10 are subdivisions of component 2 and sum to its total. Components 11–14 are subdivisions of component 3 and sum to its total. Environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) The environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) is defined as the difference in ELUC between simulations using transient and pre-industrial carbon densities (transient minus pre-industrial). Positive values indicate higher ELUC under transient carbon densities, and negative values indicate lower ELUC. Annual estimates are provided for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR in two files: GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_global_1850-2025.xlsx: Global estimates for 1850–2025 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr). GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_gridded_1959-2025.nc: Gridded estimates for 1959–2025 (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area). For OSCAR, country-level estimates were spatially disaggregated to a 0.25° grid using the spatial patterns of gross emissions and gross removals from BLUE (see Supplementary Section S.2.2 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Data underlying Figure 8 The file GCB2026_Figure8_Data.xlsx contains the datasets used in Figure 8 (a-c) of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr), within the period 1990–2025 for bookkeeping estimates and the sink in managed forests and for the period 2000–2025 for national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs; 2024 data replicated in 2025) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset groups and variables are as follows: Bookkeeping models (BMs) and peat datasets net-eluc (net ELUC): Component 1 in the above list. clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): Component 7 in the above list. other-transitions (other transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between shrubland, herbaceous vegetation, cropland, pasture, and urban areas, corresponding to the sum of components 5, 9, 10, 13, and 14 in the list above. forest (fluxes on forest land): CO2 fluxes on forest land, including permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation, net CO2 fluxes from shifting cultivation in forests, and net CO2 fluxes from wood harvest & other management, corresponding to the sum of components 4, 8, 11, and 12 in the above list. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): Component 6 in the above list. National greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) Inventory estimates are from Melo et al. (2026). net-lulucf-flux (net LULUCF flux): Net CO2 fluxes from land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires). Emissions from drainage of organic soils and fires on organic soils. other-transitions (other non-forest land uses): Net CO2 fluxes from cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements, and other land, including land remaining in these categories and transitions between them. Emissions from organic soils are reported under peat-emissions. forest (fluxes on forest land): Net CO2 fluxes from forest land remaining forest land and land converted to forest land, including harvested wood products and excluding organic soils. Dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) managed-forest-sink: The CO2 sink in managed forests estimated by DGVMs (see Supplementary Sections S.2.4 and S.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Atmospheric inversions net-lulucf-flux: The net LULUCF flux estimated by atmospheric inversions (see Supplementary Section S.2.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). description: This repository includes the data displayed in the LULUCF Data Hub, an online platform hosted by the EU Forest Observatory. It compiles various datasets of country-level CO₂ and non-CO₂ emissions and removals from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF). The LULUCF Data Hub is described by Melo et al. (ESSD Discussion). The NGHGI LULUCF database is compiled and maintained by the European Commission (EC) Joint Research Centre (JRC) and was first described by Grassi et al. 2022. It includes CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes from LULUCF sourced from the National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (NGHGIs) submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), using methodologies established by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes reported by countries in IPCC categories and sub-categories are allocated to the classes Forest (excl. organic soils, excl. HWP), Deforestation (conversion of forest land to other land uses), Other non-forest land uses, Organic soils, and Harvested wood products (HWP) (see Box 1). In the LULUCF Data Hub, and through a multi-disciplinary collaboration, we show results from global key initiatives estimating anthropogenic land use GHG fluxes translated to conceptually align with NGHGI and IPCC Guidelines definitions. In version 4.1.0 we present CO₂ data from carbon cycle modelling (Global Carbon Budget, GCB 2026; Friedlingstein et al., ESSD Discussion), CO₂ and non-CO₂ data from Global Nature Watch (formerly Global Forest Watch, GNW 2026; update of Gibbs et al., 2025), and CO₂ data from EDGAR LULUCF (Rossi et al., ESSD Discussion). Data is available in Mt CO₂ yr⁻¹ and, where available, Mt CO₂e yr⁻¹. Net CO₂ fluxes include emissions by sources and removals by sinks; non-CO₂ emissions, where available, are reported separately. Countries are identified by their ISO3 code. In addition, the timeseries files also include aggregated estimates for World (WRD) and the European Union (EU27). description: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget — 2026 Release This dataset provides gridded terrestrial biosphere model output from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional Scale Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, contributing to the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026). TRENDY is an international model intercomparison project that brings together simulations from dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) to investigate the global terrestrial carbon cycle and its response to environmental change, including atmospheric CO₂, climate variability and land-use change. This release contains the final gridded model output submitted for GCB2026. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability. Experimental design and simulations The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026. The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions: Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed S1 Transient Fixed Fixed S2 Transient Transient Fixed S3 Transient Transient Transient S4 Fixed Fixed Transient S5 Transient Fixed Transient S6 Fixed Transient Transient Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers. Changes introduced in GCB2026 In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses. For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover. The land carbon sink is calculated as: SLAND = S3 − (S4 − S0) + δL where δL represents the transient environmental effects on land-use change emissions, estimated using bookkeeping models - and can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902 The contributions from atmospheric CO₂ and nitrogen deposition and from climate are estimated as: CO₂ and nitrogen deposition: S3 − S6 + δL Climate: S3 − S5 + S0 These simulations provide a consistent framework for investigating terrestrial carbon fluxes under historical changes in environmental conditions and land use. Further methodological details are provided in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 Supplementary Information. Data availability Access and download the data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ The complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. The underlying NetCDF model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. This Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination The TRENDY-GCB2026 simulations were contributed by international modelling groups. The creators listed in this record include the TRENDY coordinators and a representative of each contributing model. TRENDY coordination: Stephen Sitch, Pierre Friedlingstein and Mike O'Sullivan. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. Release information This dataset corresponds to TRENDY version 15, the final version of the land model simulations used for the Global Carbon Budget 2026. Please use the naming convention "TRENDY-GCB2026" in publication/presentations. The Zenodo deposit contains the following files: trendy_listofvariables_GCP2026.xlsx — definitions and specifications of model output variables. TRENDY-GCB2026-manifest.csv — inventory of externally hosted gridded model output files, including filenames, paths, sizes and modification dates. TRENDY-GCB2026-model-credits.csv — contributing models, model representatives and TRENDY coordinators. TRENDY-GCB2026-data-policy.md — data usage, attribution and co-authorship requirements. The underlying gridded model output is hosted on Wasabi and is accessible through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. These model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. How to cite this dataset When using the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output, users should cite all three of the following resources: Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the terrestrial carbon sink. TRENDY model intercomparison: Sitch et al. (2024) — This publication describes the TRENDY model intercomparison framework and its application to understanding the terrestrial carbon cycle. [https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102] TRENDY-GCB2026 dataset: O'Sullivan et al. (2026) — TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget, version v15. Zenodo. [10.5281/zenodo.23561904]. This dataset record provides access to the gridded model output and formally credits the participating modelling groups. These three citations are complementary and should be included when publishing analyses based on the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output. Users should also cite relevant individual model publications where appropriate. Citation of these resources does not replace the TRENDY data policy, including the requirements for prior circulation of manuscripts and invitations to co-authorship where the data make a significant contribution. Data use and licensing The underlying model output is provided through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser and remains subject to the TRENDY data policy, including its acknowledgement, attribution and co-authorship requirements. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the TRENDY coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate. The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies only to the documentation and metadata deposited on Zenodo. It does not apply to the underlying gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the TRENDY data policy governs use and redistribution. The TRENDY data policy and model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ Related publication Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data, XX, XXXX–XXXX. [LINK] Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated terrestrial carbon sink estimates derived from the DGVM ensemble, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal: https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026 The ICOS data supplement and the TRENDY gridded model output are complementary resources. The former provides the published Global Carbon Budget synthesis results, while the latter provides access to the underlying spatially resolved terrestrial model simulations.

description: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center's SeaWiFS Project (Sea-viewing Wide Field-of-view Sensor) is utilized to measure bio-optical properties of our global oceans. Located on Orbiting Sciences Corporationメs (OSC) SeaStar spacecraft, the SeaWiFS instrument collects ocean color data. The satellite has a sun synchronous orbit at 705 km above the earthメs surface and collects data in eight wavelength bands and two telemetry streams. The Global Area Coverage (GAC) sensor gathers data in a 1502 km-wide swath with a resolution of 4.5 km, whereas the Local Area Coverage (LAC) encompasses a 2801 km-wide swath with 1.1 km coverage. LAC data is used on this site. A Sea-Air-Land Modeling and Observing Network (SALMON) Project. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

description: Zooplankton samples collected between September 8 and October 6, 2002 as part of the BASIS survey by the F/V Northwest Explorer . A total of 44 rope trawl stations were sampled along the Aleutian chain in the Bering Sea basin or within the proximity of the Aleutian Islands and stations on or adjacent to the Eastern Bering Sea shelf. Zooplankton were collected using a bongo net (mesh sizes: 333 and 505 microns) towed obliquely between the surface and 200 meters, or 20 meters from the sea floor. Zooplankton samples were split onboard the vessel with a Matoto splitter and sample halves were preserved in formalin and frozen. Formalin preserved specimens have been sent to the Polish sorting center for species identification; frozen specimens will be used for stable isotope analysis. Surface water samples were collected and filtered for stable isotopes, coccolithophores, and chlorophyll. Filters were frozen and 250 ml of the filtered water was retained for nutrient analysis (NO 2 , NO 3 , PO 4 , and SiO 3 ). [Reference: Murphy, J., N. Davis, O. Ivanov, M. Rohr, S. Elmajjati, and W. Barber. 2003. Cruise report of the 2002 F/V Northwest Explorer BASIS survey in the Bering Sea, September- October. (NPAFC Doc. 676 Rev. 1) 23 p. NMFS, Auke Bay Laboratory, Juneau, AK; School of Aquatic& Fishery Sciences, University of Washington; Pacific Fisheries Research Centre (TINRO-Centre), Vladivostok; Alaska Quaternary Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks; Institute of Marine Science, University of Alaska Fairbanks.] This report is available at http://www.npafc.org/restricted_doc/2003%20Documents_PDF/676(Rev1)(USA).pdf Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

description: This repository provides Part 2 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering November 2022 to July 2026. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 2 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 1, covering May 2018 to October 2022, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23463271).

This is a draft release of annual national emissions accounts based on extracted fossil fuels and carbonates: emissions from oxidation of the fuels (or venting of fossil CO2) and decomposition of the carbonates (only in cement so far) are allocated to the country that extracted them regardless of where in the world oxidation / venting / decomposition occurs. These can be seen as a complement to territorial and consumption-based emissions (as well as emissions aligned with National Accounts). Estimates are derived from energy data published by the Energy Institute, Mohr et al. (2014), UN Statistics Division, JODI, and the Global Carbon Budget (for both flaring/venting and cement). Where available, national emissions are reported from 1850, while the per capita series starts in 1950. These start years may be pushed back to earlier periods in future releases. The final year of data is 2025. As a draft release, there are some issues with the estimates. For example, in some years the global total is less than the sum of the individual countries reported. Further, while the global totals are in general very close to the territorial emissions estimates in GCP's fossil CO2 dataset, there are some divergences. These things will be worked on as time permits.

# Data and code for "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" Version 1.0 (2026-10-23) This archive contains all data products of the study "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" and the code that produced them. Using SWOT lake observations densified with Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery, we observed storage changes at 1,447 reservoirs in 96 countries during 5,399 floods between August 2023 and August 2026, and corrected the bias from sparse satellite sampling with daily in-situ storage from the USA, Brazil and Australia. The median reservoir retained about one third of the flood inflow (corrected retention ratio 0.33; raw satellite lower bound 0.22). ## Contents ``` reservoir_flood_retention_v1.0.zip ├── README.md this file ├── dataset/ data products of the study (about 47 MB) │ ├── README.md field-by-field documentation │ ├── D1_flood_events.csv │ ├── D2_storage_series.zip │ ├── D3_pld_grand_map.csv │ ├── D4_calibration_pairs.csv │ ├── D5_cama_scenarios.zip │ └── D6_cama_obs_module.zip └── code/ full processing code and the data needed to redraw the figures (about 82 MB) ├── README.md workflow and usage ├── LICENSE ├── scripts/ ├── data/ └── figures/ ``` ### dataset/ | File | Content | |---|---| | D1_flood_events.csv | Flood-event retention dataset (core product): 5,399 floods × 88 fields, including raw and corrected retention ratios, pre-flood headroom, GloFAS reservoir-module retention and reservoir attributes | | D2_storage_series.zip | Reservoir storage time series: SWOT-only (3,033 reservoirs) and SWOT + optical fused (2,938 reservoirs) | | D3_pld_grand_map.csv | Lookup between the SWOT Prior Lake Database and GRanD: 12,729 lakes matched to 6,719 reservoirs | | D4_calibration_pairs.csv | Satellite–in-situ calibration pairs: 732 floods at 171 reservoirs | | D5_cama_scenarios.zip | CaMa-Flood v4.3 results for seven reservoir scenarios at dam sites and downstream | | D6_cama_obs_module.zip | Observation-constrained CaMa-Flood reservoir module (Fortran), daily input tables and run scripts | D2, D5 and D6 are themselves zip files because they contain many files or large tables; unzip them where needed. See `dataset/README.md` for every field. ### code/ Scripts for the full workflow, in eight steps: | Folder | Step | |---|---| | scripts/01_swot | SWOT download, lake–reservoir matching, storage series, water-level validation | | scripts/02_optical | Sentinel-2/Landsat water-area extraction and fusion with SWOT | | scripts/03_glofas_events | GloFAS inflow, return periods, flood event detection | | scripts/04_insitu | In-situ data download (USACE CWMS, BoM, ONS) and in-situ checks | | scripts/05_calibration_drivers | Bias correction and analysis of controlling factors | | scripts/06_cama | CaMa-Flood forcing, observation-constrained module, scenario runs and comparison | | scripts/07_figures | Main figures | | scripts/08_release | Dataset release package | `code/data/` contains the inputs needed to redraw the four main figures. To redraw them: ```bash cd code/scripts/07_figures python fig_main_v8.py ``` The output PNGs are byte-identical to the figures in the paper. See `code/README.md` for the full workflow, the software environment (Python 3.9; gfortran for CaMa-Flood) and the raw data that must be downloaded separately (SWOT, GloFAS, ERA5-Land; several hundred GB in total). ## How the two folders relate - `dataset/` holds the final data products; `code/` holds the scripts that produce them and a copy of the intermediate tables needed for the figures. - `code/scripts/08_release/make_release.py` builds the files in `dataset/` from the full working data. - The Python scripts and run scripts inside `dataset/D6_cama_obs_module.zip` are identical to those in `code/scripts/06_cama/`. - All tables are linked by the GRanD reservoir identifier `GRAND_ID`; flood events are identified by `event_id` (`GRAND_ID_peakdate`). ## Main caveats 1. The bias correction is trained on in-situ data from the USA, Brazil and Australia only; applying it elsewhere is an extrapolation. The raw satellite retention ratio (`ret_wm`) is provided as a lower bound. 2. Single-event corrected retention ratios are uncertain; aggregate by reservoir, region or group. 3. All analyses use SWOT observations with quality flag good (quality_f = 0). The SWOT-only series in D2 also keep suspect observations (quality_f = 1), which should normally be removed. 4. In-situ reservoir records from USACE, ONS and BoM, and the flood storage capacity estimates of Shen et al. (2025), are not redistributed. ## Licences | Part | Licence | |---|---| | Data in `dataset/` and `code/data/` | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) | | Scripts written for this study in `code/scripts/` | MIT (`code/LICENSE`) | | Files derived from CaMa-Flood (`code/scripts/06_cama/fortran/`, `code/scripts/06_cama/gosh/`, and the module and run scripts in D6) | Apache License 2.0, as the original CaMa-Flood code (licence text in `code/scripts/06_cama/LICENSE-Apache-2.0.txt` and in D6) | Third-party sources must also be cited under their own terms: SWOT LakeSP (doi:10.5067/SWOT-LAKESP-D), GloFAS v4 and ERA5-Land (Copernicus), GRanD and Global Dam Watch, GRDL (doi:10.1029/2023WR035781), GROWL (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31225405), Sentinel-2 and Landsat, and the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators.

Consists of satellite measurements of global and regional ocean color data obtained by the Sea-viewing Wide Field-of-view Sensor, in orbit on the OrbView-2 (formerly SeaStar) platform. The concentration and predominant identity of substances and particles in the euphotic (lighted) zone of the upper ocean influences the apparent color of the ocean, which can range from deep blue to varying shades of green and ruddy brown. Living phytoplankton (which contain chlorophyll and associated photosynthetic pigments), inorganic sediments, detritus (particulate organic matter), and dissolved organic matter all contribute to the color of the ocean. The data are primarily intended for used by marine researchers. All SeaWiFS data files are in Hierarchical Data Format (HDF). [ Reference: PICES Scientific Report No. 18 2001, Proceedings of the PICES/CoML/IPRC Workshop on "Impact of Climate Variability on Observation and Prediction of Ecosystem and Biodiversity Changes in the North Pacific", http://www.pices.int/publications/scientific_reports/Report18/default.aspx. ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

description: A global ocean color data set derived from satellite observations. In most oceanic regions, the color of the ocean is primarily determined by the abundance of phytoplankton and their associated photosynthetic pigments. As phytoplankton pigment concentration increases, ocean color gradually shifts from blue to green. NASA developed the CZCS to utilize this characteristic of ocean color for the observation of pigment distribution in the oceans. The CZCS was launched on the Nimbus-7 satellite in October 1978. During the 91 months of its operation (October 1978 - June 1986), CZCS acquired nearly 68,000 images, each covering up to 2 million square kilometers of ocean surface. Data can be obtained directly at ftp://daac.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/czcs. [ Reference: PICES Scientific Report No. 18 2001, Proceedings of the PICES/CoML/IPRC Workshop on "Impact of Climate Variability on Observation and Prediction of Ecosystem and Biodiversity Changes in the North Pacific", http://www.pices.int/publications/scientific_reports/Report18/default.aspx. ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

description: Borneo's mangroves share one coastline, one climate and one sediment regime, yet they are governed by three countries. Using the annual Global Mangrove Watch v4.1 series and open data, this study asks why mangrove in Indonesian Kalimantan is lost faster than in Malaysian Borneo and Brunei, and tests three explanations: protected-area performance, conversion pathways and El Niño sea-level fall. Between 2010 and 2020, Kalimantan lost 1.23% of its mangrove a year, against 0.43 to 0.74% in Malaysian Borneo and 0.50% in Brunei; it held 59% of the island's mangrove and 77% of its gross loss. Matched comparisons show long-standing strict protected areas reduced loss in Malaysian Borneo by about 2 percentage points but had no detectable effect in Kalimantan. Protection nonetheless explains little of the gap: 84% of it arises in unprotected mangrove, and Sabah's 2015 upgrades of low-loss production reserves to full protection added nothing measurable. Classifying what replaced mangrove lost from 2000 to 2024 shows that conversion to aquaculture ponds, concentrated in the early 2000s, accounts for all of Kalimantan's 15.9-point excess loss, while loss away from ponds was similar in total on both sides of the border (clearing in Kalimantan and Sarawak, mostly edge change in Sabah) and oil palm replaced little mangrove. Annual loss outside conversion was lowest in El Niño years and highest in high-sea-level years, consistent with humid mangroves buffered against El Niño sea-level fall. Reducing Borneo's mangrove loss therefore depends on governing pond expansion in unprotected mangrove more than on adding protected areas. Keywords: Mangrove loss; aquaculture; protected areas; Borneo; El Niño; Global Mangrove Watch

description: A global census of mangrove extent on a 10 km equal-area grid (EPSG:6933), derived from Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) v4.1.12, for 2025 with change since 2015. Each 10 km cell containing mapped mangrove carries its 2025 fill fraction, mangrove area, 2015–2025 change and a watch-priority tier (A/B/C/dust). Headline results: 25,682 cells contain mapped mangrove in 2025, holding 150,675 km² (raw pixel area; GMW's published 2025 total converted the same way is 150,674 km²). 7,847 cells hold 90% of the world's mapped mangrove and 1,722 hold half. 1,350 cells lost at least 0.5 km² and at least 5% of their mangrove between 2015 and 2025. Contents: 2015 and 2025 fill-fraction rasters (GeoTIFF), the change raster, a GeoPackage of all cells with fill, area, change and tier, CSV summaries, two charts, the scripts that generate everything, SHA-256 checksums of the outputs and of the 1,696 GMW input tiles, and a README with the method, quality checks and limitations. The tiers are a watch-priority ranking for monitoring, not a finding of deforestation: a drop in mapped mangrove may be clearing, natural change or mapping error. Accuracy is inherited from GMW v4.1.12. Derived from Global Mangrove Watch v4.1.12 (CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21346457); please cite both.

description: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - 2026 Release This dataset provides surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs), surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products) and the ocean inverse model OCIM (interior ocean observationally-constrained estimate). Types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series (2) one file per GOBM and simulation (A, B) with gridded fields (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations (4) the gridded file of the natural steady state fluxes from simulation B of six GOBMs that exclude riverine fluxes and have a globally-integrated natural steady state CO2 flux within ± 0.2 GtC yr-1. This data is used to subtract the natural steady state fluxes from the fCO2-products in regional anaylses (Figures 14 and 15) (5) A file for the gridded CO2 fluxes and one file for the global time-series of the ocean inverse model OCIM (simulations C and B) that is used as an observationally-constrained interior ocean data-product in GCB. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2026, are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 spreadsheet (https://globalcarbonbudget.org/datahub/). The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2026 paper, the river flux adjustment needs to be added and an adjustment for the natural steady state fluxes needs to be subtracted from the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (River flux adjustment: North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2026 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Three of the ten fCO2-products (UExP-FFN-U, JMA-MLR and AOML-ET) include a temperature adjustment to correct the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files. fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude (3) One file 'GCB2026_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. (4) One file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_1959_2025.nc) that contains the gridded field and one file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc) that contains the global time-series of CO2 fluxes of OCIM for simulations C and B. Further data availability: Access and download the additional data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ In addition to the zenodo deposit, the complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. In addition to the data described above, this Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination: The GCB2026-OCEAN data sets were contributed by international research groups. The creators listed in this record include the GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators and a representative of each contributing data set. GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators: Judith Hauck and Peter Landschützer with support from Simone Le Chevère and Alizée Roobaert. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. How to cite this dataset When using the GCB2026-OCEAN data, users should cite both of the following resources: Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the ocean carbon sink. GCB2026-OCEAN dataset: Hauck et al. description: This dataset contains the data and analysis code supporting a comparison of CLCD v1.0.5 and GLC_FCS30D v2 along urban riverfronts in Fuzhou, Guangzhou, Hangzhou and Nanning, China. The study uses the 2010 and 2020 classifications for one predefined 15 km main-river reach in each city. The files include land-cover windows, frozen study geometries and class mappings, pixel- and edge-level records, derived tables, GIS layers, and source code. The analyses cover product-specific land–water interfaces, strictly paired interface states, and land-cover transitions in two landward distance bands. Supplementary workflows examine common source classes, proximity between interfaces, reference water geometry, leave-one-segment-out sensitivity, and half-cell shifts of the analysis grid. Figure source data and the submitted supplementary tables are also included. The historical-imagery records contain the acquired Landsat and Sentinel windows, source metadata, archived AI observations, and eligibility decisions. No two-date trajectory met the predefined main-reference criteria; these records therefore do not provide an independent estimate of either product’s accuracy. The README identifies the calculation entry points and software requirements. File checksums and execution records document the archived inputs and the checks performed when preparing this deposit. Third-party data retain their original licences and source attribution.
keywords: urban riverfronts; land-cover products; CLCD; GLC_FCS30D; land-water interface; product sensitivity

description: High-resolution surface PM2.5 concentration for India, built from satellite products, surface monitors, and machine learning pipelines. This dataset is produced using a reimplementation of Improved daily PM2.5 estimates in India reveal inequalities in recent enhancement of air quality (Kawano, et al., 2025) built by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). See southasia-pm2-5.energyandcleanair.org for more details. You can download daily PM2.5 data from the original authors for 1 January 2005 to 30 September 2023 from https://zenodo.org/records/13694585. Structure of the dataset The dataset is provided in CF-1.8–compliant NetCDF format, containing daily surface PM2.5 concentrations (µg/m³) at 10 km resolution over India. It includes time, x, and y dimensions, with the primary variable pm25(time, y, x). The data uses the WGS 84 / India NSF Lambert Conformal Conic projection (EPSG: 7755) to define spatial coordinates. Filenames and the meaning of each version field are described in the additional notes on this record. Model accuracy We provide the results of the spatial cross-validation in a CSV file alongside the results. This has the headers r2 and rmse (in µg/m³). We use the same cross-validation metrics and methodology for daily values as for the final full model by Kawano et al. (2025). Using the data When using this data, please reference: Kawano, Ayako, et al. “Improved daily PM2.5 estimates in India reveal inequalities in recent enhancement of air quality.” Science Advances 11.4 (2025): eadq1071. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adq1071 The version of the data used from Zenodo.

This dataset provides global monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°, with the latest update extending through September 2026. The dataset is designed to provide a valuable resource for assessing the global carbon budget and the effectiveness of climate mitigation efforts. The estimates are generated using a deep learning–based framework that employs a convolutional neural network as its backbone and incorporates a mask fusion module to address spatially missing input data. The framework integrates satellite observations, meteorological reanalysis data, and temporal and spatial encoding features to estimate anthropogenic CO₂ emissions at a global scale. The data are provided in NetCDF format on a global 0.1° × 0.1° grid (1800 × 3600 cells) using the WGS84 geographic coordinate system. Each file contains monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates for all 12 months of a given year, expressed in tonnes month⁻¹ cell⁻¹. Files follow the naming convention ACO2_01deg_YYYY.nc, where YYYY denotes the corresponding year. The dataset is also updated regularly at doi: 10.12237/casearth.6a01788fe8a21d1686165027 A manuscript describing the methodology and dataset is in preparation.

description: We randomly defined 44 sites for which approximately 1000 points were randomly stratified using the mangrove / non-mangrove proportions of the scene. description: Overview This record contains the de-identified eco-hydrological restoration benchmark used to evaluate PG-RAMEO (Physics-Guided Regime-Aware Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization), a surrogate-assisted many-objective framework for climate-adaptive wetland restoration. The benchmark couples two-dimensional Saint–Venant shallow-water hydrodynamics with multi-decadal vegetation, salinity and soil-organic-carbon succession across 240 wetland restoration units spanning three geomorphological archetypes (Floodplain Marsh, n = 96; Coastal Estuarine, n = 84; Depressional Peatland, n = 60) under three hydro-climatic forcing regimes (Historical, CMIP6 SSP2-4.5, CMIP6 SSP5-8.5). Source data and de-identification. Hydrological boundary conditions, bathymetric depths, porewater salinity gradients and archetype proportions are anchored to three public monitoring repositories: the USGS Everglades Depth Estimation Network (EDEN) and NWIS (sofia.usgs.gov/eden, waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis), the CAMELS catchment dataset (ral.ucar.edu/solutions/products/camels), and the Global Lakes and Wetlands Database GLWD v2 / HydroSHEDS (hydrosheds.org/products/glwd). All station identifiers and geographic quasi-identifiers have been replaced by randomized hash codes (WRU_xxxx), calendar dates are omitted, and the spatial partition is encoded in the split column (train = 144, val = 36, test = 60). Contents data/processed/ — granular evaluation records (8 files, 8,315 data rows): wetland_basins_metadata.csv — 240 rows. Physical, hydrological and biogeochemical attributes of every restoration unit: area, drainage area, cell count, control structures, inflow, mean depth, hydroperiod, reference evapotranspiration, salinity, initial biomass, soil organic carbon, Manning roughness, bathymetric discontinuity, critical salinity (22.5 ppt) and anoxic (42.0 d) thresholds, and sensor missing rate. method_basin_regime_evaluations.csv — 5,760 rows (240 units × 3 regimes × 8 methods). Four-objective hypervolume (hv), igd_plus, candidate and feasible counts, ecological regime violation counts by mechanism (salinity_violations, anoxia_violations, desiccation_violations), surrogate state errors (rmse_h, rmse_biomass, mass_balance_err), individual objective scores (obj_hsi, obj_ncsr, obj_faee, obj_lcec), and computational speedup. seed_level_test_runs.csv — 720 rows (30 seeds × 3 regimes × 8 methods) on the held-out test split, the input to all paired significance tests. ablation_basin_evaluations.csv — 1,440 rows across the eight variants (Full, Abl-C1, Abl-C1b, Abl-C2, Abl-C2a, Abl-C2b, Abl-C3, Backbone). surrogate_operator_grid.csv — accuracy and mass-balance consistency of seven neural and statistical operator architectures. sensitivity_sweep_grid.csv — sweeps over flux weight λflux ∈ [0.0, 2.0], high-fidelity query ratio ρHF ∈ [0.05, 0.20], repair step ηrep ∈ [0.02, 0.40] and solver budget BHF ∈ [60, 480]. pareto_front_solutions.csv — representative non-dominated solutions per method. regime_shift_trajectories.csv — monthly coupled state trajectories (S(t), h(t), B(t)) over a 36-month SSP5-8.5 compound drought–flood sequence, comparing unrepaired offspring, random-mutation repair and CR-FEH directional physics-Jacobian repair. data/derived/ — the summary tables behind every reported result (7 files, 182 rows): main_table.csv (primary comparison on val and test), regime_archetype_table.csv (subgroup breakdown), ablation_table.csv, surrogate_consistency_table.csv, sensitivity_table.csv, dataset_summary_table.csv, and failure_mode_breakdown.csv (violation counts by physical failure mechanism under SSP5-8.5). Every file in data/derived/ is regenerated deterministically from data/processed/ by the companion code record. Reuse Released under CC BY 4.0. If you use these data, please cite this record together with the associated article. The columns obj_hsi, obj_ncsr, obj_faee and obj_lcec denote habitat suitability index, net carbon sequestration rate, flood attenuation efficiency and lifecycle engineering cost respectively; ehr_fr is the ecological regime feasibility ratio.
keywords: surrogate-assisted evolutionary optimization; multi-fidelity graph neural operator; physics-informed neural networks; shallow-water equations; wetland eco-hydrological restoration; climate adaptation; wetland restoration benchmark; multi-objective optimization

description: Overview This dataset provides harmonised annual fractional land cover representations derived from ESA Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (ESA CCI LC) and GLC_FCS30D for the Mediterranean area. The original categorical land cover legends were reclassified into ten broad, FAO LCCS-compatible classes, following the thematic harmonisation approach described by Bratic et al. (2023), and aggregated to a common 0.1-degree latitude-longitude grid. Each valid grid cell contains class-specific fractional cover values between zero and one, describing the mapped composition rather than a single dominant class. The datasets support cross-product comparisons of multi-temporal land cover composition. Fractions remain dependent on the accuracy and temporal characteristics of their original source products. Included files cci_reclass_lc_fractions_1992_2022.nc - ESA CCI LC-derived fractional land cover dataset (nominal coverage 1992-2022) glc_reclass_lc_fractions_1985_2022.nc - GLC_FCS30D-derived fractional land cover dataset (the source maps are annual from 2000 to 2022, with earlier maps in 1985, 1990 and 1995). GLANCE_LC_Fractions_User_Guide_v1.pdf - technical documentation including the complete thematic crosswalk. Data structure and methods NetCDF variables: `forest`, `shrubland`, `grassland`, `cropland`, `wetland`, `lichens_and_mosses`, `bareland`, `built_up`, `water`, `permanent_ice_and_snow`. Dimensions: `year`, `y`, `x`. Coordinate reference system: EPSG:4326. Nominal grid: 0.1 degrees; fractional values are dimensionless in [0, 1]. No-data source pixels are excluded from the valid-pixel denominator. For the full legend and reclassification rules, refer to the User Guide. Project context Developed within ESA GLANCE (AGricultural Land AbandoNment and ClimatE change) project, which investigates Mediterranean agricultural land abandonment and its interactions with forest dynamics and water, energy and carbon cycles. Project: https://climate.esa.int/en/Cross_ECV_Projects/glance. Source datasets and required attribution ESA CCI Land Cover / Copernicus Climate Data Store: https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.006f2c9a. The applicable ESA CCI LC source licence requires explicit credit to the ESA Climate Change Initiative Land Cover project. Licence text: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/licences/satellite-land-cover GLC_FCS30D: Liu, L., Zhang, X., and Zhao, T. (2023), original Zenodo version v1, DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8239305. Licence: CC BY 4.0. Associated data description: Zhang et al. (2024), Earth System Science Data, DOI: https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-1353-2024 Thematic harmonisation reference: Bratic, G., Oxoli, D., and Brovelli, M. A. (2023). Map of Land Cover Agreement: Ensambling Existing Datasets for Large-Scale Training Data Provision. Remote Sensing, 15(15), 3774. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15153774. Rights and re-use The GLC-derived component is subject to GLC_FCS30D CC BY 4.0 upstream attribution. The CCI-derived component is subject to the ESA CCI Land Cover licence, which explicitly allows educational/scientific use with attribution but does not explicitly establish unrestricted commercial redistribution.

This record contains the data and the code of the main calculations of a study that compares the daytime and nighttime land surface temperature (LST) of urban water bodies, green spaces and built-up land in 229 Chinese cities on a 1 km grid (June–August, 2018–2023). Contents: data/cells_1km.csv.gz: 746,554 cells of 1 km with LST by day and night, water occurrence, vegetation and built-up shares, elevation, background air and dewpoint temperature, NDVI, evapotranspiration and residents; data/cities.csv: the 229 cities with their aridity index and zone and summer climate; data/results/: city-level and station-level results underlying the figures and tables of the paper; code/: Python code of the main calculations (cooling intensity, the adjusted advantage of Eq. 1, the cover effects of Eq. 2 and the water demand), with a README that lists the variables, sources and steps. Source datasets: Global Urban Boundaries, MODIS Aqua LST (MYD11A2, MYD11A1), ESA WorldCover v200, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land, TerraClimate, MODIS NDVI (MOD13A2), ET (MOD16A2GF) and albedo (MCD43A3), PML-V2.2a, Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2, WorldPop 2020, gridded GDP per capita (Kummu et al., 2025) and the Integrated Surface Database. Only derived values are included; the source data are available from their providers. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information 2026.

description: Trait data, analysis code and result tables for the hollow-versus-solid stem-architecture dimension of the grasses (Poaceae; Cyperaceae as a solid-stemmed outgroup). DATA: 12,208 Poales species (11,602 Poaceae + 606 Cyperaceae) with stem hollowness and woodiness states compiled from Kew GrassBase, Flora of China (iPlant) and the official Flora of North America Poaceae treatment (2,054 species with documented stem state, 1,448 of them grasses); species- and genus-level environment (GBIF coordinates, WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids, with CHELSA V2.1 and TerraClimate cross-checks, Last-Glacial-Maximum anomalies and the Global Aridity Index v3); an 11,287-tip Open Tree phylogeny with fossil-calibrated time-tree derivatives; and the result tables behind every manuscript number. CODE: the final analysis and figure chain (phylogenetic logistic regression, dual-axis independence tests, ancestral states, HiSSE/BiSSE diversification, Euler biomechanics, hydraulic bounds, environment PCA, coverage/resolution sensitivity matrices), the regex-extraction protocols for all grass sources, the LLM-extraction protocol of the eudicot screen, and the PCD expression-screen subproject. Entry points: run_all_analyses.sh / reproduce_analyses.sh (R 4.5: phytools, phylolm, MCMCglmm, caper, ape; Python 3.13, see requirements.txt; HiSSE fits included as RDS). NOT REDISTRIBUTED: raw floristic texts, rasters, GBIF downloads, source trees and RNA-seq reads (licensing and size). License: CC BY-NC 4.0 (data and code).

This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP. From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it. The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1); • The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp); • Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted); • Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution. NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts. A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code. Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010.

description: Bolivia Fire version 0.1.0 provides a weekly VIIRS S-NPP standard-processing satellite-detection benchmark for Bolivia and its retained reproduction evidence. The strict panel contains 37,146 cells, 678 Monday issues from 2013-01-07 through 2025-12-29 and 25,184,988 cell-weeks. The target is a selected satellite detection, not a count of fires, ignitions or burned area, and is not an official warning. Three independently extractable ZIP64 archives use repository-relative paths: benchmark-data: panel, cells, CHIRPS rainfall, MOD13A2 vegetation, MapBiomas Collection 4 land-cover and combined features, schemas and manifests. reproduction-artifacts: configurations, environment lockfile, fitted models and calibrators, retained predictions and alternative-learner cached vectors, evaluation history, figure JSON, family-specific producing revisions and historical source registries. raw-inputs: FIRMS CSV snapshots, MOD13A2 AppEEARS subset, CHIRPS native windows, MapBiomas aggregate exports, boundaries, GeoNames and outage HTML. Top-level README, licence notices, data dictionary, member inventory and SHA-256 checksums describe the files. Dataset reuse is supported. Recalculation from saved predictions is partially supported: strict primary validation/test exports and alternative-learner cached vectors are retained; rainfall, sensitivity and vegetation, land-cover and combined covariate per-row prediction exports and standalone scored-row masks are absent. Their result records and fitted models remain available. Recomputing any final-test metric is a logged test opening under the frozen protocol; release verification does not open the test. Rebuilding from raw inputs is partially supported. Global CHIRPS rasters, MODIS HDF granules and native MapBiomas 30 m maps are not supplied; MapBiomas re-extraction requires an Earth Engine account. Operational live forecasts, serving derivatives, regenerable caches, temporary files and logs are excluded. Later environmental experiments are separate from the original CHIRPS comparison; retained 2026 availability evidence does not establish a completed confirmation evaluation. Known discrepancies include an older unmatched cell-place manifest hash, fourteen unretained intermediate states, the MOD13A2 acquisition AOI buffer of 0.05 degrees versus the registered 0.1 degrees, and CatBoost GPU digit-level nondeterminism. See the record README for details and producing-code revisions. Load serialized model files only from trusted sources. Compiled and derived data are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Upstream raw inputs retain NASA open-data/public-domain or attribution terms detailed in LICENSES.md, including CHIRPS, MapBiomas and GeoNames CC BY 4.0 and GeoBolivia public-domain boundaries. Code is separately MIT licensed at Cupesi/bolivia-fire. Cite the dataset version and the software separately.

description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal and Tibet. We provide here pre-event and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from Pléiades, SPOT6 and SPOT5 stereo-images. Date were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES. The collection includes three files: Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_pre-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_post-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_dh.tif =========================== Methods The post-event DEM is purely based on Pleiades stereo images. The pre-event DEM is based mostly Pléiades and SPOT6 stereopairs. A small fraction of the pre-event DEM was derived from 10 m SPOT5-HRS images. All DEMs were generated at a ground sampling distance of 4 m using the semiglobal matching algorithm of the Ames Stereo Pipeline (Beyer et al., 2018; Shean et al., 2016) and the processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). A ground sampling distance of 10 m was used for SPOT5-HRS. All individual DEMs were first co-registered and vertically adjusted to the Copernicus 30 (GLO-30) DEM, masking out glaciers using the Randolph Glacier Inventory v7 (RGI 7.0 consortium, 2023). Next, the individual pre- and post-event DEMs were co-registered in pairs to construct the most accurate DoD possible. Finally, those individual DoDs were mosaicked in a single map of elevation difference. The uncertainty on the mean elevation change was calculated using the patch method (Dussaillant et al., 2018). This approach aims to empirically determine the uncertainty associated with the mean elevation change by sampling patches (or tiles) of stable terrain of various sizes to constrain the decay of error with increasing averaging area (Miles et al., 2018; Wagnon et al., 2021). The stable terrain was defined here as excluding glaciers and a buffer around the river channels where erosion or deposition has occurred. For a 1 km² averaging area, the 1-sigma (68th percentile) error and the 2-sigma (95th percentile) error were calculated to be ±0.8 and ±1.8 m, respectively. Beyer, R. description: This dataset provides the result tables and the analysis code underlying the article "From phantom to functional: riparian agroforestry insetting for fruit-eating migratory fish" (submitted to Academia Environmental Sciences and Sustainability). The study starts from the climate refugia identified for two fruit-eating migratory fishes of the Parana-Paraguay Basin, Piaractus mesopotamicus and Myloplus tiete, in do Couto et al. (2026), Academia Biology 4(2), doi 10.20935/AcadBiol8362. Within the 1935 refugia cells of 10 km that require riparian restoration, it maps the riparian vegetation deficit in 100 m buffers, estimates the potential carbon dioxide sequestration, compares the 20-year net present value of passive regeneration, assisted regeneration and agroforestry with yerba mate and native fruit trees, and ranks micro-basins into investment tiers with a composite insetting index. The dataset contains three parts. 1. Refugia cells (GeoPackage, EPSG:6933). The 1935 cells of 10 km x 10 km that require riparian restoration, with the attributes inherited from the previous study. 2. Tables (CSV and JSON). Riparian vegetation deficit per micro-basin and landscape composition per cell; current and reference above-ground biomass, soil organic carbon and potential carbon dioxide sequestration of the 450,512 riparian pixels of 1 ha, with centroid coordinates; for the 171,192 restorable pixels with carbon gain, the climatic suitability of yerba mate, the land opportunity cost, the net present value of the three scenarios, the internal rate of return and the payback period; the 10,000 Monte Carlo draws and the Sobol indices of the economic assumptions; the five sub-indices and the composite insetting index per pixel; and the index, carbon, net present value and investment tier of the 2462 micro-basins. A pixel identifier links all pixel tables, and micro-basins are identified by the HydroBASINS level 10 code. 3. Code. The Python and Google Earth Engine scripts of the five phases of the analysis, of the successive re-runs and of the figures, including the final economic analysis (spatial land cost, suitability-scaled revenue, Monte Carlo simulation and Sobol decomposition) and the script that audits the consistency of the results. Monetary values are given in Brazilian reais and in United States dollars, converted at R$5.4443 per USD (mean PTAX selling rate of the Central Bank of Brazil from 16 October 2024 to 15 October 2026). The input datasets (HydroRIVERS, HydroBASINS, MapBiomas, ESA CCI Biomass, SoilGrids, JRC Global Surface Water, Global Dam Watch, GBIF and WorldClim) are not redistributed and are available from their providers. The dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY 4.0). Please cite this dataset and the associated article.
keywords: insetting; riparian restoration; agroforestry; yerba mate; climate refugia; ichthyochory; carbon sequestration; nature's contributions to people; Monte Carlo; Paraná–Paraguay Basin

description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Rasuwa region in Nepal and Tibet : https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/ We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades stereo acquired on the 16 October 2022, 4 years before the event.
